scenario: Your team automates a nightly invoice-processing job. Every invoice goes through the exact same four steps in the exact same order: OCR the PDF, extract fields into JSON, validate against the PO database, and write a row to the ledger. There is no branching and no open-ended decision-making; the steps never change. Leadership wants the most reliable, lowest-cost, easiest-to-debug implementation.
stem: What architecture best fits this task?

options.text: A conversational assistant that asks a human to confirm each step
A deterministic workflow that calls each step as code in sequence, using the model only for the OCR/extraction step
A fully autonomous agent that decides at runtime which step to run next
A peer-to-peer multi-agent system where each step is an agent negotiating with the others

explanation: The steps are fixed, ordered, and have no dynamic decisioning, so a deterministic workflow is the simplest thing that works: predictable, cheap, and easy to debug. The model is only needed where genuine NL/vision understanding is required (OCR/extraction). C adds agentic autonomy with zero benefit and worse predictability/cost. D is the most complex topology and is unjustified when steps don't need to negotiate. A inserts a human in a loop that is already fully automatable, defeating the goal of an unattended nightly job.

scenario: An orchestrator agent must produce a market report by researching 6 competitors. Early prototypes had each research step run inline in the orchestrator's own context. After a few competitors, the orchestrator started hallucinating and mixing up facts because its context window was crammed with raw web pages, tool logs, and intermediate reasoning from every competitor.
stem: What change best fixes the context-pollution problem?

options.text: Increase the orchestrator's max_tokens (output limit) so it can emit longer responses
Switch the orchestrator to a peer-to-peer topology so the research steps talk to each other
Delegate each competitor to a subagent that runs in its own isolated context window and returns only a short structured summary to the orchestrator
Have the orchestrator re-read all raw pages at the end and summarize them in one pass

explanation: The hub-and-spoke pattern with subagents provides context isolation: each subagent processes its raw materials in a separate window and returns only its result, so the orchestrator never accumulates the noise. A raises the output token cap, which does nothing about input-context pollution and still keeps all the raw pages crammed into one window. B adds inter-agent communication that doesn't address the root cause (too much raw data in one context) and increases complexity. D keeps every raw page in the orchestrator's context, the exact failure mode being observed.

scenario: A document pipeline has four sub-tasks: (1) translate the doc to English, (2) summarize the translated English text, (3) extract named entities from the translation, and (4) sentiment-score the translation. Tasks 2, 3, and 4 each consume the output of task 1, but none of them depends on each other.
stem: What is the most efficient correct execution plan?

options.text: Run task 1 first, then run tasks 2, 3, and 4 in parallel
Run tasks 2, 3, 4 in parallel first, then run task 1
Run all four tasks strictly sequentially in the order 1-2-3-4
Run all four tasks fully in parallel from the start

explanation: Task 1 is a hard dependency for the others, so it must complete first; tasks 2-4 are mutually independent and can be parallelized to save wall-clock time. D is wrong because 2-4 would run before their input (the translation) exists. C produces correct output but is needlessly slow, serializing three independent tasks. B inverts the dependency, running consumers before the producer.

scenario: A coding agent occasionally tries to run destructive shell commands like 'rm -rf' or push directly to main. Prompt instructions telling it not to do this work most of the time but fail under unusual phrasings. You need a hard guarantee that these specific commands are blocked, and when blocked you want the agent to understand why so it can choose a safer path.
stem: What is the most reliable way to enforce this?

options.text: Add stronger wording to the system prompt forbidding destructive commands
Add a PostToolUse hook that logs destructive commands after they execute
Add a PreToolUse hook that returns a generic nonzero exit code other than 2
Add a PreToolUse hook that inspects the command and returns exit code 2 with an explanatory message on stderr when it matches a banned pattern

explanation: Hooks are deterministic code-level enforcement, and exit code 2 specifically blocks the action and feeds stderr back to Claude so it can self-correct, which is exactly the 'block and explain' behavior required. A relies on the model complying, which is the failure mode being fixed. B runs PostToolUse, after the destructive command has already executed, so it provides no prevention. C blocks via the wrong code path: a nonzero code other than 2 is treated as a non-blocking error, so the command is not reliably blocked and stderr isn't fed back as a block.

scenario: A customer-facing agent that issues account refunds receives a request: 'Reverse the charge from last week.' The customer has three charges in the last week of materially different amounts, and a wrong refund is costly and hard to claw back. The agent's confidence in which charge is meant is low.
stem: What is the best-designed agent behavior here?

options.text: Pick the most recent charge and proceed silently without confirming
Ask a clarifying question (or escalate) to disambiguate which charge before taking any refund action
Refund all three charges to be safe and reconcile later
Refund the largest charge since that is most likely what the customer cares about

explanation: With genuine ambiguity and high, hard-to-reverse stakes, the correct pattern is to clarify or escalate rather than guess. D, C, and A all guess on an irreversible, costly action: D and A pick a single interpretation with no basis and act silently, while C compounds the error by issuing refunds the customer never requested. The reliability doctrine is to resolve ambiguity and escalate on low confidence / high stakes.

scenario: You are designing a content-creation system: a planner breaks a brief into sections, several writer agents draft sections independently, and an editor assembles and polishes the result. The writers never need to coordinate with each other; they only need their assigned section spec and return finished prose. The team wants the most controllable and debuggable topology.
stem: Which topology should you choose?

options.text: A single monolithic agent that writes all sections in one context window
Peer-to-peer: every writer agent communicates directly with every other writer to coordinate
Hub-and-spoke: an orchestrator delegates section specs to writer subagents and collects their results, then passes to the editor
A pipeline where each writer feeds its draft as input to the next writer in a chain

explanation: Writers are independent and only need a spec in and prose out, which is the textbook hub-and-spoke case: a central orchestrator delegates and collects results, giving clean control and context isolation. B (peer-to-peer) adds direct inter-agent communication that the writers don't need and that is the hardest topology to control. A loses the parallelism and context isolation benefits and risks context pollution across sections. D (pipeline) imposes a false sequential dependency between writers who are actually independent, serializing work and coupling drafts unnecessarily.

scenario: A code-fixing agent applies a patch to make a failing test pass. In production it frequently reports success while the test still fails, because it edits the file and immediately declares the task done without checking.
stem: Which change most directly addresses the failure?

options.text: Lower the temperature so the agent's edits are more deterministic
Add an explicit verify step to the loop: after editing, run the test suite and only finish if it passes, otherwise replan and retry
Increase the context window so the agent can see more of the codebase
Give the agent a more capable model so its first edit is more likely correct

explanation: The defect is a missing verify phase of the agentic loop (gather -> act -> verify -> repeat); adding a real verification gate (run the tests, loop on failure) directly fixes premature success claims. D and A may marginally improve first-attempt quality but provide no guarantee and don't add verification, so the agent can still declare success on a still-failing test. C gives more context but doesn't make the agent check its own work; without verification the same false-success behavior persists.

scenario: Stakeholders want a tool that lets analysts ask ad-hoc questions about a dataset in a back-and-forth chat, with a human reviewing and steering after every model turn. The number and nature of follow-up questions is unpredictable and entirely human-driven.
stem: Which system type is the best fit?

options.text: A conversational assistant with a human in the loop on each turn
A fully autonomous agent that runs a long unattended loop
A hub-and-spoke orchestrator delegating each question to a fleet of subagents
A fixed batch workflow that runs once and returns a static report

explanation: The interaction is human-driven turn-by-turn with review at each step, which is precisely a conversational assistant. B removes the human-in-the-loop the stakeholders explicitly want and is built for unattended autonomy. D is a one-shot deterministic path that cannot support unpredictable ad-hoc follow-ups. C is heavyweight orchestration for what is fundamentally a single interactive dialogue, adding cost and complexity with no benefit.

scenario: A research agent built its plan assuming a particular API would return company financials. Mid-run, that API starts returning 404s for half the companies. The agent currently keeps calling the dead endpoint and eventually returns a half-empty report without flagging anything.
stem: What is the best behavior to engineer into the agent?

options.text: Detect the tool failures, replan to use an alternate data source, and if none works, surface the gap explicitly in the output rather than silently returning incomplete data
Abort the entire run on the first 404 with no partial results and no explanation
Retry the same failing endpoint indefinitely until it succeeds
Catch the 404s and silently substitute zeros so the report is fully populated

explanation: Good agent design verifies tool outputs, replans when reality diverges from the plan, and propagates errors explicitly instead of swallowing them; surfacing the gap when no alternative works is correct error propagation. D silently fabricates data (zeros), which is the dangerous 'swallow the error' anti-pattern. C is a degenerate non-replanning loop that never adapts. B throws away usable partial work and still fails to communicate what went wrong, the opposite of explicit, graceful error propagation.

scenario: A data-quality system must process records through three stages where each stage strictly transforms the previous stage's output: normalize -> deduplicate -> enrich. Stage N cannot start until stage N-1 has produced its full cleaned output, and each stage has a distinct specialized prompt and tool set.
stem: Which multi-agent topology matches this structure?

options.text: A single agent doing all three stages with one shared prompt and toolset
Three agents running fully in parallel from the start
A peer-to-peer mesh where all three agents continuously exchange partial results
A pipeline of three specialized agents, each consuming the prior stage's output

explanation: Strict stage-to-stage data dependencies with distinct specialized prompts/tools is the defining case for a pipeline topology: sequential stages, each feeding the next. B is impossible given the hard dependencies (dedup can't run before normalize finishes). C adds continuous bidirectional communication that the linear dependency doesn't require and is the hardest topology to reason about. A collapses three specialized roles into one generalist context, losing the focused prompts and least-privilege tool scoping that the staged design provides.

scenario: You must build an agent that, given a vague request like 'improve our onboarding,' should produce a prioritized action plan. The work involves an unknown number of steps, branching that depends on what it discovers (e.g., reading docs, interviewing systems, checking metrics), and no two runs look the same. Cost is a secondary concern to handling open-endedness well.
stem: What is the most appropriate architecture?

options.text: A fixed workflow that hardcodes the exact sequence of steps in code
An agent that dynamically directs its own process and tool use, decomposing the task at runtime and replanning as it learns
A conversational assistant that returns whatever the first model turn produces with no tool use
A batch job that runs the same static template prompt over all inputs

explanation: Unknown step count, discovery-dependent branching, and high run-to-run variance are exactly the conditions where you add agentic autonomy: let the model direct its process, decompose at runtime, and replan. A can't work because the steps cannot be enumerated in advance. C does no tooling or iteration and so can't do the multi-step research the task requires. D applies one rigid template to inherently non-uniform inputs, the opposite of the dynamic decomposition needed.

scenario: An agent built with the Agent SDK runs long migration tasks that can take hours and sometimes get interrupted (machine restarts, rate limits). The team wants to resume an interrupted run from where it left off instead of restarting from scratch, and wants each migration's state kept separate.
stem: Which capability of the Agent SDK best supports this requirement?

options.text: Running every migration inside the same shared session to reuse context
Resumable sessions: capture each migration's session id and resume from it, so the SDK reloads that conversation's persisted state and each migration stays in its own session
Increasing max_tokens so the whole migration finishes in one response
Prompt caching of the system prompt so re-runs are cheaper

explanation: The Agent SDK persists each session's conversation state to disk and lets you resume by session id, which is exactly what 'continue an interrupted run' needs, and a separate session per migration keeps each one's state isolated. D reduces input cost on repeated stable prefixes but does nothing to persist or resume progress. C is irrelevant: max_tokens caps a single response's length, not multi-hour task continuation, and can't survive a restart. A shares one session across migrations, mixing their state together, which violates the requirement to keep them separate.

scenario: In your orchestrator-subagent system, one subagent only needs to read files and summarize them, while another needs to execute shell commands and write to the repo. Currently all subagents inherit the same broad tool allowlist, and the read-only summarizer has occasionally been induced by malicious file content to run shell commands.
stem: What is the best design fix?

options.text: Give each subagent its own least-privilege tool allowlist, so the summarizer subagent has no shell or write tools at all
Keep the shared allowlist but add a prompt instruction telling the summarizer not to run shell commands
Keep full tool access on every subagent but route execution requests through the orchestrator for logging
Merge the two subagents into one so there is a single allowlist to manage

explanation: Subagents can each have their own tool allowlist, and scoping tools to least privilege is the recommended practice; removing shell/write tools from the summarizer makes the prompt-injection class of attack structurally impossible for it. B relies on the model obeying instructions, the exact thing prompt injection defeats. D couples a read-only role with a high-privilege role, enlarging the attack surface rather than reducing it. C leaves every subagent, including the summarizer, holding full tool access, so an injected command can still execute regardless of orchestrator logging.

scenario: A team proposes a five-agent peer-to-peer system to answer FAQ-style support questions by looking up answers in a single knowledge base. In testing, a single agent with one retrieval tool answers the same questions just as accurately, faster, and at a fraction of the cost. The team still wants to ship the multi-agent design because it 'feels more advanced.'
stem: What is the right architectural recommendation?

options.text: Ship the five-agent peer-to-peer system because more agents generally yield higher quality
Ship both and let them vote on each answer
Ship the single agent with one retrieval tool, since it is the simplest design that meets the requirements
Ship a hub-and-spoke version of the five agents as a compromise

explanation: The governing principle is to prefer the simplest thing that works; the single agent matches accuracy while being faster and cheaper, so the added agents are pure overhead. A is the classic 'more agents = better' fallacy; multi-agent systems add coordination cost and unpredictability and are only justified when the task needs them. D still pays for five agents and an orchestrator to solve a problem one agent already solves. B doubles cost and latency to ensemble two solutions where one already suffices, again violating the simplicity principle.

scenario: A 40-engineer fintech team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. The security org has set an enterprise/policy CLAUDE.md mandating that no code may call external HTTP endpoints in test files. One engineer, Priya, has a personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md preferring tabs over spaces. The repo's committed ./CLAUDE.md says 'use 2-space indentation' to match the linter. Priya notices Claude keeps producing 2-space indentation despite her user-level preference, and she wants to understand the resolution rules before filing a complaint.
stem: Which explanation of the precedence behavior is correct, and what is the right architectural takeaway?

options.text: The files combine, but more specific (project-level ./CLAUDE.md) instructions override more general (user-level) ones for the indentation conflict, so the 2-space project rule wins; the enterprise policy still sits above both and cannot be overridden by either.
User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md always wins because it is loaded last, so Priya's tabs should take effect; the project file is being ignored due to a bug.
Only one CLAUDE.md is ever active at a time, so the project file completely replaces the user and enterprise files, meaning the security policy is not being applied.
Enterprise policy is lowest priority because it is the most general, so the project file overrides it; Priya should escalate to remove the project file.

explanation: Correct (A): The hierarchy is enterprise/policy -> user -> project -> project-local, where more specific overrides more general, and files combine rather than replace. The project ./CLAUDE.md (more specific than user) wins the indentation conflict, while enterprise policy remains authoritative on top. B is wrong: user-level does not win conflicts against project-level; project is more specific. C is wrong: files combine, they do not mutually exclude, so the security policy still applies. D inverts the hierarchy: enterprise/policy is the HIGHEST authority, not the lowest, and cannot be overridden by a project file.

scenario: A platform team wants to guarantee that Claude Code never runs `git push --force` against the protected main branch during autonomous sessions. They write a PreToolUse hook that inspects the Bash tool command. They are debating how the hook should signal a hard block so that Claude both stops the action AND learns why, so it can choose a safer alternative on its own.
stem: How should the hook be designed to deterministically block the action and let Claude self-correct?

options.text: Exit with code 1 and write the reason to stdout, which guarantees a hard block and surfaces the reason to the model.
Exit with code 2 and write the explanation ('force-push to main is forbidden; use a PR') to stderr, so the action is blocked and the message is fed back to Claude.
Return the block as a tool_use error inside the model's context window instead of using the hook exit code, since hooks cannot block tool calls.
Exit with code 0 but print a warning to stdout, trusting Claude to honor the warning and skip the push.

explanation: Correct (B): In Claude Code hooks, exit code 2 blocks the action and feeds stderr back to Claude so it can self-correct (confirmed in the official hooks reference: for PreToolUse, exit code 2 blocks the tool call and stderr is fed back to Claude). D is wrong: exit 0 is success/non-blocking, so the push would proceed, and on exit 0 Claude does not even see stdout (except UserPromptSubmit); relying on the model to 'honor a warning' defeats the deterministic guardrail. A is wrong: exit 1 (other nonzero) is a NON-blocking error whose stderr is shown to the user while execution continues, and the reason must go to stderr, not stdout. C is wrong: PreToolUse hooks are precisely the deterministic mechanism that CAN block tool calls, which is the whole point of using a hook rather than hoping the model complies.

scenario: A data team built a Skill that converts messy CSVs into a normalized internal schema. They wrote SKILL.md with frontmatter `name: csv-normalizer` and a one-line description: 'Helper for data tasks.' In practice Claude almost never invokes it, even when an engineer says 'normalize this raw CSV export into our schema.' The bundled instructions and reference tables are excellent once it loads, but it rarely loads.
stem: What is the most effective fix, given how Skills are selected and loaded?

options.text: Rewrite the YAML `description` to be specific and trigger-rich (e.g., 'Normalize raw/messy CSV exports into the internal canonical schema; use when converting, cleaning, or mapping CSV columns'), because Skills trigger by description match.
Rename the Skill to `aaa-csv-normalizer` so it sorts first and is selected before other skills.
Convert the Skill into a CLAUDE.md section so it is always loaded into every session regardless of the task.
Move all the reference tables into the description field so Claude always has them in context and is more likely to use the Skill.

explanation: Correct (A): Skills trigger by description match, so a vague description ('Helper for data tasks') fails to match user intent; making it specific and keyword-rich is the highest-leverage fix. D is wrong and counterproductive: progressive disclosure means the description should be lean for matching while detail loads only when needed; stuffing tables into the description bloats every prompt and does not improve triggering. C defeats progressive disclosure by forcing the content into every session, wasting context. B is a superstition: selection is by description relevance, not alphabetical sort order.

scenario: An engineer is building a large refactor workflow in Claude Code. A 'security-auditor' subagent needs to read the entire dependency tree and produce a one-paragraph risk verdict, while the main orchestrator continues planning the refactor. The engineer worries that the auditor's huge intermediate reading will pollute the orchestrator's context and blow the token budget. They define the auditor in `.claude/agents/security-auditor.md`.
stem: Which property of subagents most directly solves the engineer's concern, and how should the auditor be configured?

options.text: Subagents cannot read files independently; the orchestrator must read the dependency tree itself and pass the contents into the subagent, which is what keeps context clean.
Subagents always inherit every tool the orchestrator has, so the only way to limit pollution is to reduce the orchestrator's own toolset before launching the auditor.

Subagents run in isolated context windows, so the auditor's large intermediate reading stays in its own context and only its final verdict returns to the orchestrator; give it its own prompt and a least-privilege tool allowlist in the agent file.
Subagents share the orchestrator's context window, so the engineer must manually summarize the auditor's reading; configure a hook to truncate the context after the audit.

explanation: Correct (C): Subagents run in isolated context windows; the auditor's bulky reads never enter the orchestrator's context, and only its result returns. Subagents defined in .claude/agents have their own prompt and a tool allowlist, so least-privilege scoping is appropriate. D is wrong: subagents do NOT share the orchestrator's window; that is the entire benefit. B is wrong: subagents have their own configurable tool allowlist, so you scope the subagent directly, not by crippling the orchestrator. A is wrong: subagents can use their own tools (including reading files) within their isolated context; forcing the orchestrator to read everything would defeat isolation and pollute its context.

topic: headless / non-interactive -p for CI/CD with JSON output
scenario: A team wants Claude Code to run in their GitHub Actions pipeline to triage failing tests and post a structured summary to a downstream job. The pipeline step must be non-interactive, must emit machine-parseable output that the next step can `jq` over, and must not wait for any human prompt.
stem: What is the correct invocation pattern for this CI step?

options.text: Use the Batch API endpoint from inside the runner since CI is non-latency-sensitive, bypassing Claude Code entirely.
Launch the interactive TUI and rely on plan mode to auto-exit when finished, capturing the terminal scrollback as the artifact.
Run `claude` with no prompt and feed keystrokes via an expect script, then screen-scrape the colored output.
Use headless mode: `claude -p "triage the failing tests and summarize" --output-format json`, piping the JSON to the next step for parsing.

explanation: Correct (D): `claude -p "..."` is the headless/non-interactive mode designed for CI/CD and scripting, and `--output-format json` yields machine-parseable output to pipe downstream. B is wrong: plan mode is a read-only research/plan mode, not a CI auto-exit mechanism, and scraping scrollback is fragile. C is wrong: driving the interactive TUI via expect and screen-scraping is exactly what `-p` exists to avoid. A conflates two different things: the Batch API is an Anthropic Messages API feature for bulk async jobs, not the way you run the Claude Code agent in a pipeline; the question is about Claude Code, not raw API batching.

scenario: A senior engineer is about to let Claude Code work on a critical production billing service. Before any files are touched, she wants Claude to investigate the codebase, map the call graph, and propose a step-by-step change plan that she can review and approve, with a hard guarantee that no edits happen during this phase.
stem: Which Claude Code capability is the right fit for this 'investigate-and-propose-without-editing' phase?

options.text: Headless `-p` mode, which is inherently read-only and cannot modify files.
A PostToolUse hook that reverts every file edit after it happens, simulating read-only behavior.
A subagent, because subagents are read-only by definition and cannot write.
Plan mode, which is a read-only research/planning mode that lets Claude explore and propose a plan before any edits are made.

explanation: Correct (D): Plan mode is explicitly a read-only research/plan-before-editing mode, exactly matching the requirement. B is a hacky workaround: PostToolUse fires after an edit, so files would be modified then reverted, not prevented, and is error-prone. A is wrong: `-p` headless mode is about non-interactive execution, not read-only safety; it can absolutely make edits. C is wrong: subagents are not inherently read-only; they have configurable tool allowlists and can be granted write tools.

scenario: A team repeatedly types the same long multi-paragraph prompt to generate a conventional-commit message from the current diff. They want a reusable, version-controlled shortcut named `/commitmsg` that every team member gets automatically when they clone the repo.
stem: What is the correct way to implement this shortcut in Claude Code?

options.text: Add the prompt to `.claudeignore` so Claude treats it as a reusable command.
Create a Markdown file `commitmsg.md` in `.claude/commands/` containing the prompt template; it becomes the `/commitmsg` custom slash command and is committed with the repo.
Define it as a SKILL.md so it triggers automatically without anyone typing a command.
Register it as a PreToolUse hook so it runs the prompt before each Bash command.

explanation: Correct (B): Custom slash commands are Markdown files in .claude/commands; a `commitmsg.md` there yields `/commitmsg` and, being in the repo, is shared on clone. A is wrong: .claudeignore controls which files Claude can access, not command definitions. C is a misuse: Skills trigger automatically by description match, but the team wants an explicit user-invoked command, which is exactly what a slash command is. D is wrong: hooks are deterministic lifecycle callbacks, not user-invoked prompt templates.

scenario: A repo contains a `secrets/` directory with rotated credential fixtures and a massive `vendor/` directory of third-party code that bloats context and confuses Claude. The team wants Claude Code to never read the secrets and to avoid pulling vendor files into context, while still allowing normal work on `src/`.
stem: What is the appropriate mechanism, and what does it actually control?

options.text: Add `secrets/` and `vendor/` to `.claudeignore` (and/or deny rules in settings), which controls which files Claude can access so they are excluded from reads and context.
Use a PostToolUse hook to delete any secret file Claude reads, preventing leakage after the fact.
Move the secrets into a subagent's context window, since subagent context is isolated and therefore private from the orchestrator.
Put the exclusions only in CLAUDE.md as instructions ('please never read secrets/'), relying on the model to comply since no access-control mechanism exists.

explanation: Correct (A): .claudeignore and access settings control file access, so listing secrets/ and vendor/ excludes them from reads and from context bloat, which is exactly the requirement. D is wrong: a CLAUDE.md instruction relies on model compliance and is not the access-control mechanism, and the claim that no access control exists is false. B is wrong and dangerous: PostToolUse fires after the read, so the secret would already be in context, and deleting files is destructive. C is nonsense for this goal: subagent context isolation is about not polluting the orchestrator, not a vault for storing secrets you want excluded from access.

topic: hooks lifecycle events (PreToolUse vs PostToolUse vs Stop)
scenario: A team has three policy needs: (1) prevent edits to any file under `migrations/` unless a ticket ID is present, (2) automatically run `prettier --write` on any file right after Claude edits it, and (3) emit a Slack notification when Claude finishes responding for the turn. They want each enforced deterministically at the right lifecycle moment.
stem: Which mapping of needs to hook events is correct?

options.text: (1) PreToolUse to inspect and potentially block the edit before it happens; (2) PostToolUse to format the file after the edit; (3) Stop to notify when Claude finishes the turn.
(1) PostToolUse to block the edit after inspecting it; (2) PreToolUse to format the file before the edit; (3) PreToolUse again to notify on completion.
All three should be Stop hooks, since Stop is the only event that can read tool arguments and results.
(1) Stop to block migrations edits at end of turn; (2) Stop to format; (3) PostToolUse to notify, because notifications must follow a tool call.

explanation: Correct (A): PreToolUse runs before a tool executes, so it is where you inspect and (via exit 2) block a disallowed migration edit; PostToolUse runs after the edit, the right place to auto-format; Stop fires when Claude finishes responding, the right place for a turn-completion notification. B inverts blocking and formatting: you cannot block an edit after it already happened, and formatting must run after, not before, the edit. C is wrong: Stop is not the only event with access to tool context, and it fires at end of turn, far too late to block a specific edit. D misuses Stop for per-edit blocking/formatting (wrong timing) and misroutes the turn-completion notification to PostToolUse.

topic: Agent SDK agentic loop and workflows vs agents
scenario: A team must process 10,000 invoices nightly with an entirely fixed sequence: OCR -> field extraction -> schema validation -> write to DB. The steps never branch, the inputs are uniform, cost matters, and predictability is paramount for the finance auditors. A junior engineer proposes building a fully autonomous agent with the Agent SDK that 'figures out what to do' for each invoice.
stem: What is the best architectural decision per the agents-vs-workflows guidance?

options.text: Implement a deterministic workflow (predefined code path) for the fixed pipeline; reserve agentic autonomy for the rare open-ended exceptions that genuinely need dynamic decisioning.
Use a hub-and-spoke orchestrator that spawns a fresh subagent per invoice to maximize parallelism, regardless of the fixed steps.
Build a fully autonomous agent for every invoice, because agents are always more capable than workflows and the SDK is designed for autonomy.
Put the entire pipeline inside a single giant prompt and let the model decide ordering each night, since fewer moving parts means more reliability.

explanation: Correct (A): When steps are fixed and predictability/cost matter, a workflow (deterministic, predefined code path) is preferred; you add agentic autonomy only where dynamic decisioning is actually needed. C is the classic over-engineering mistake: agents are more flexible but less predictable and more expensive, and the guidance is to prefer the simplest thing that works. B adds orchestration complexity and nondeterminism for a task that has no branching; parallelism can be achieved without making each unit autonomous. D wrongly conflates 'fewer components' with reliability; letting the model re-decide a fixed order each night reduces determinism, the opposite of what auditors need.

scenario: An engineer returns to a complex microservices repo after three weeks. The previous Claude Code sessions discovered non-obvious architecture decisions, a tricky build gotcha, and a recurring bugfix pattern. She wants Claude to reliably carry that hard-won context into the new session without her re-explaining everything, and she wants the durable facts that every future session should respect to be enforced.
stem: Which combination correctly separates durable session-spanning instructions from regenerable distilled knowledge?

options.text: Store the durable rules in .claudeignore so they are protected from edits, and discard the distilled knowledge.
Put everything, including volatile distilled observations, directly into CLAUDE.md so it is all loaded every session.
Rely solely on the model's memory of prior sessions; CLAUDE.md is only for indentation preferences.

Put authoritative, always-apply rules and conventions in the project ./CLAUDE.md (committed), and keep regenerable distilled observations in a separate file like .claude/distilled-knowledge.md so the two do not conflict.

explanation: Correct (D): Durable, must-respect rules belong in the committed project CLAUDE.md, while regenerable distilled knowledge is kept separate (e.g., .claude/distilled-knowledge.md) to avoid conflicts and churn in the authoritative file. B over-stuffs CLAUDE.md with volatile content, causing churn and conflicts and wasting context. C is wrong: there is no reliable cross-session model memory to depend on, and CLAUDE.md is for far more than indentation. A misuses .claudeignore, which controls file access, not rule durability, and discarding the distilled knowledge throws away the value.

scenario: A platform team is packaging an internal 'release-runbook' Skill. The full runbook is 4,000 lines covering dozens of edge cases, version matrices, and rollback scripts. They are worried that bundling all of it will balloon every session's context, but they also need the depth available when an actual release is underway.
stem: How should the Skill be structured to respect progressive disclosure?

options.text: Put the entire runbook into the YAML `description` field, since the description is what gets matched and loaded.
Keep SKILL.md lean with a precise triggering description and high-level steps, and reference the detailed runbook material so the deep content is loaded only when the Skill is actually needed.
Split the runbook across 30 separate Skills, one per edge case, so each is tiny, accepting that triggering becomes ambiguous.
Inline all 4,000 lines into SKILL.md so Claude always has the full runbook resident in context.

explanation: Correct (B): Progressive disclosure means the Skill exposes a lean description and entry instructions for matching, and loads detailed material only when needed, which keeps context lean while preserving depth on demand. D defeats progressive disclosure by making the full runbook always-resident, bloating context. C fragments the Skill so much that description-based triggering becomes ambiguous and selection degrades. A is a misunderstanding: the description is for matching and must stay concise; it is not a dumping ground for full content, and overloading it harms triggering and wastes tokens.

topic: Stop hook as a deterministic guardrail
scenario: A team requires that every Claude Code session that modifies code must end only after the test suite passes. Engineers keep forgetting, and sometimes Claude declares it is done while tests are red. The team wants a code-enforced rule that, when Claude tries to end the turn with failing tests, prevents completion and tells Claude what is still broken so it keeps working.
stem: What is the most robust mechanism to enforce 'don't finish until tests pass'?

options.text: A Stop hook that runs the test suite and, on failure, blocks completion (exit code 2) while writing the failing-test details to stderr so Claude is prevented from stopping and gets actionable feedback to continue.
Run tests only in the CI pipeline after the session, accepting that local sessions can end red.
A PreToolUse hook on the test command, so tests are validated before they run.
Add 'always run tests before finishing' to CLAUDE.md and trust the model to comply every time.

explanation: Correct (A): The Stop event fires when Claude tries to finish; a Stop hook can run tests and block completion on failure (exit code 2, with the failing details on stderr fed back to Claude, equivalently a 'block' decision with a reason) so Claude self-corrects, which is the deterministic guardrail the team wants (hooks enforce policy in code rather than hoping the model complies). D relies on model compliance, the exact thing that has been failing. C targets the wrong event: PreToolUse fires before a tool runs, not at turn completion, so it cannot enforce 'pass before finishing.' B abandons the requirement of blocking local session completion and only catches failures later in CI.

scenario: A documentation modernization project needs three parallel investigations on a large codebase: an API-surface mapper, a dead-code finder, and a test-coverage analyzer. Each produces a long intermediate transcript but the lead only needs each one's final findings. The architect wants maximum parallelism while keeping the coordinator's context small, and wants each investigator restricted to only the tools it needs.
stem: Which design best matches the orchestrator-subagent (hub-and-spoke) pattern and its benefits?

options.text: A central orchestrator delegates to three specialized subagents (defined in .claude/agents) running in parallel isolated contexts, each with a least-privilege tool allowlist, each returning only its final result rather than its full transcript.
A pipeline where the API mapper feeds the dead-code finder which feeds the coverage analyzer, since sequential stages are always more reliable than parallel ones.
A peer-to-peer mesh where all three subagents talk directly to each other and merge transcripts into the orchestrator's context for full visibility.
A single agent with every tool enabled that does all three investigations in one context window to avoid the overhead of multiple agents.

explanation: Correct (A): Hub-and-spoke is one coordinator delegating to specialized subagents in parallel, each in an isolated context returning only its result, which keeps the orchestrator's context small; defining them in .claude/agents with least-privilege tool allowlists matches best practice. B misapplies a pipeline (sequential, each feeding the next) to three INDEPENDENT investigations that should run in parallel, and 'sequential is always more reliable' is false. C is wrong: peer-to-peer plus merging full transcripts into the orchestrator defeats the goal of keeping its context small and adds coordination complexity that is not needed here. D abandons context isolation and least privilege, dumping all intermediate work into one window and over-granting tools.

scenario: Your team is building a service that turns customer support emails into structured tickets with fields like category, priority, and customer_id. Right now you ask Claude in the prompt to 'respond only with JSON,' and roughly 4% of responses include a prose preamble or a trailing markdown fence that breaks your JSON.parse step downstream.
stem: What is the most robust way to make Claude reliably emit conformant structured output?

options.text: Lower temperature to 0 and hope the format stabilizes
Add the sentence 'DO NOT include any text other than JSON' three times in the system prompt
Define a tool with an input_json_schema and have the model return a tool_use block whose input conforms to the schema
Switch to the Batch API so responses are processed offline and can be cleaned up later

explanation: C is correct: the recommended path for structured output is tool_use with an input_json_schema, which constrains the model to return a conforming input object instead of free text. B is a prompt band-aid that does not constrain shape and still produces stray text. A reduces variation but does not enforce a schema or eliminate preambles/fences. D changes how jobs are dispatched (async/cheaper) but does nothing about output format.

scenario: You ship a pipeline that extracts invoice line items into JSON via a tool with a defined schema. In production, about 1 in 200 responses still violates the schema (e.g., a quantity returned as a string, or a missing required field) and crashes the parser.
stem: What is the best way to make the extraction step resilient to these occasional schema violations?

options.text: Validate the JSON in code and, on failure, feed the specific validation error back to the model and ask it to correct, retrying until it conforms
Wrap the parser in a try/except that drops any response that fails to parse
Loosen the schema so every field is an optional free-form string, eliminating validation failures
Increase max_tokens so the model has room to finish the JSON correctly

explanation: A is the canonical validation-retry loop: validate, and on failure return the actionable error to the model for self-correction. C trades a catchable error for silent garbage and loses type guarantees. B silently drops data — propagating/correcting errors is preferred over swallowing them. D addresses truncation only; the described failures are type/required-field violations, not length cutoffs.

topic: placing long context before the query
scenario: You are building a contract-analysis feature. Each request includes a 40-page contract plus a specific question like 'What is the termination notice period?' Your current template puts the question at the very top, followed by the full contract text. Accuracy is mediocre and the model sometimes answers from generic knowledge instead of the contract.
stem: How should you restructure the prompt to improve grounded accuracy?

options.text: Summarize the contract down to one paragraph and ask the question against the summary
Keep the question first but raise temperature so the model explores the document more
Place the full contract BEFORE the question and instruct the model to quote the relevant passages first, then answer
Repeat the question every few pages throughout the contract text

explanation: C reflects two authoritative rules: put long documents before the query, and ask the model to quote relevant parts first to ground the answer. B does not fix structure and adds noise. A is risky progressive summarization that loses the exact detail (a specific notice period) you need. D clutters the middle of the context — where attention is weakest ('lost in the middle') — and does not improve grounding.

scenario: A RAG assistant stuffs 30 retrieved chunks plus a list of strict formatting rules into one large prompt. Engineers notice the model frequently ignores the formatting rules, which currently sit in the middle of the prompt between chunks 15 and 16.
stem: What change is most likely to make the model reliably follow the formatting rules?

options.text: Move the critical formatting rules to the start and/or end of the prompt rather than burying them in the middle
Bold the formatting rules and increase their font size in the markdown
Add 20 more retrieved chunks so the model has more supporting evidence
Convert the rules into a few-shot example placed in the exact middle of the chunks

explanation: A applies the 'lost in the middle' finding: models attend best to the start and end, so important instructions belong at the edges. B is cosmetic; markdown weight does not change attention. C worsens the problem by adding more middle content. D still places the critical content in the worst position.

scenario: A teammate wants every response to begin as a JSON object and proposes prefilling the assistant turn with an opening '{'. They then argue that because of the prefill, you can delete the JSON-validation step entirely.
stem: How should you evaluate this proposal?

options.text: Prefilling guarantees valid JSON, so removing validation is safe
Prefilling only works with plain-text generation and cannot be combined with a tool_use schema, so it is the wrong tool here
Prefilling usefully steers the output toward JSON, but it does not guarantee conformance, so the validation step must stay
Prefilling and tool_use are mutually exclusive, so adopting prefill means abandoning the schema

explanation: C is correct: prefilling steers format but provides no validity guarantee, so you keep validation. A overstates prefill's power. B is a plausible-sounding but false constraint — prefilling is a general format-steering technique and does not 'only work' with plain text. D invents a mutual-exclusivity rule; prefill is a steering technique that does not preclude using tool_use schemas.

scenario: You are generating regulatory disclosure summaries that a compliance officer signs off on. Errors are costly and rare cases of subtle misstatement have slipped through single-pass generation. Latency and token cost are secondary concerns for this high-stakes output.
stem: Which prompting strategy best fits this situation?

options.text: Use a multi-pass generate → critique → revise flow where a review pass explicitly checks the draft against the source before finalizing
Generate once at temperature 0 and accept it, since temperature 0 eliminates errors
Ask for the summary and a confidence score in one pass, and ship whatever has confidence above 0.5
Generate three independent drafts and concatenate them into one summary

explanation: A is the multi-pass / self-critique pattern (generate, verify, revise) recommended for high-stakes output, where the cost is justified. B is wrong: temperature 0 reduces variance, not factual error. D concatenates rather than reconciling, producing redundancy and contradictions, not verification. C ships on a weak threshold and conflates a self-reported score with actual correctness; for high stakes you verify, not just self-rate.

scenario: A classifier prompt labels user messages as one of {bug, feature_request, billing, other}. It does well on clear cases but misroutes ambiguous messages — e.g., a billing complaint phrased as 'this is broken' gets labeled 'bug.' Your three few-shot examples are all unambiguous, textbook cases.
stem: What is the most effective fix to the prompt?

options.text: Remove all few-shot examples so the model relies on its own judgment
Add few-shot examples that specifically cover the ambiguous/edge cases and show the correct label and reasoning for each
Add 50 more unambiguous examples to reinforce the clear cases
Replace examples with a longer prose paragraph describing each category in detail

explanation: B is correct: example selection should cover edge cases, which is exactly where the classifier fails. A discards a proven technique. C reinforces cases that already work and ignores the failure mode. D swaps targeted examples for prose, which is generally less effective than well-chosen few-shot examples for demonstrating the exact decision boundary.

scenario: Your extraction tool returns a 'status' field and a 'priority' field. Downstream code assumes status is one of three values and priority is an integer 1–5, but the model occasionally returns 'in-progress' vs 'in progress' or a priority of 'high', breaking joins and sorts.
stem: What schema change best prevents these inconsistencies at the source?

options.text: Constrain status to an enum of the exact allowed string values and define priority as an integer with an explicit min/max range in the schema
Merge status and priority into a single string field to reduce schema complexity
Keep both as free-form strings and normalize them with a post-processing regex
Make both fields optional so the model can omit them when unsure

explanation: A applies tight schema design: enums pin closed string sets and a bounded integer type enforces priority, eliminating the variants at generation time. C pushes the problem downstream and is brittle as new variants appear. B destroys the structure you need and complicates downstream logic. D makes the data sparser and does not constrain the values that are present.

scenario: A prompt concatenates a knowledge-base article, a set of style rules, and the user's question as one undifferentiated block of text. The model sometimes treats the style rules as content to summarize, or quotes the user's question back as if it were source material.
stem: What is the cleanest way to eliminate this confusion between instruction and data?

options.text: Add line breaks between the sections and hope the model infers their roles
Wrap each part in clearly named XML tags (e.g., <article>, <style_rules>, <question>) so roles are unambiguous
Move everything into the system prompt so it all has the same authority
Increase max_tokens so the model has room to keep the sections straight

explanation: B uses XML tags to delimit and label distinct context, the recommended technique for removing instruction-vs-data ambiguity. A relies on inference, which is exactly what failed. C collapses meaningful role distinctions and would make the model treat data as standing instructions. D is unrelated to sectioning.

scenario: A math-word-problem grader must output a strict JSON object {answer, is_correct}. You find that letting the model reason improves accuracy, but when you allow free reasoning the reasoning text leaks into the JSON and breaks parsing.
stem: How do you keep the accuracy benefit of reasoning without corrupting the structured output?

options.text: Have the model reason in a separate <thinking> section and return the final structured answer via the tool_use schema, parsing only the tool input
Lower temperature to 0, which removes the need for any reasoning
Ask the model to put its reasoning inside the JSON 'answer' field and strip it later
Forbid all reasoning so the output stays clean, accepting the accuracy loss

explanation: A separates chain-of-thought (in a thinking section) from the parsed structured answer (tool_use input), preserving reasoning benefits without polluting the output. D sacrifices accuracy unnecessarily. C deliberately mixes reasoning into the data field, the very corruption you are trying to avoid. B conflates determinism with reasoning ability; temperature 0 does not replace step-by-step reasoning.

scenario: A summarization prompt just says 'Summarize this document.' Stakeholders complain the summaries are inconsistent — sometimes one sentence, sometimes a page, sometimes missing the action items they care about.
stem: What is the highest-leverage prompt change?

options.text: Switch from Sonnet to Opus so the model is smart enough to guess the intent
Run the same prompt three times and average the outputs
Append the vague, self-contradictory instruction 'be concise but thorough' to the end of the prompt
State explicit success criteria: target length, required sections (including action items), tone, and what to exclude

explanation: D directly addresses the root cause: the prompt never defined what good looks like. Being explicit about success criteria is the core lever. A throws model capability at an underspecified spec; a better model still cannot read unstated requirements reliably. B cannot average free-text summaries meaningfully. C is vague and internally contradictory ('concise but thorough'), not an explicit, measurable criterion, so it will not stabilize length or guarantee action items.

scenario: You extract structured fields from clinical notes where missing or fabricated values are dangerous. The model occasionally invents a plausible value (e.g., a dosage) when the note does not actually state it.
stem: Which combination of techniques best reduces fabrication in this extraction task?

options.text: Tell the model 'do not hallucinate' in the system prompt and trust it
Raise temperature so the model considers more possibilities before extracting
Require the model to quote the exact supporting span for each field and return null when no supporting text exists, validated by a schema that allows null
Drop the schema and ask for a prose narrative that you parse heuristically

explanation: C combines quote-the-source grounding with an explicit null path and schema validation, the recommended way to reduce fabrication and keep provenance. B increases randomness, which makes invented values more likely. A is an unenforced instruction with no grounding mechanism. D removes the structure and validation entirely, worsening reliability.

scenario: Two engineers debate how to return a nested object {customer:{id,name}, items:[{sku,qty}]}. One wants to paste the desired JSON shape as text in the prompt and ask the model to 'follow this shape exactly.' The other wants to encode that shape as a tool input_json_schema.
stem: Which approach should the team prefer for reliable nested structured output?

options.text: Encode the shape as a tool input_json_schema so the model's tool_use input is constrained to that structure
Paste the JSON shape as text, because describing it in the prompt gives the model more flexibility
Ask the model to return YAML instead, which is easier to validate than JSON
Return a flat key-value list and reconstruct nesting in code to avoid schemas

explanation: A is the recommended approach: a tool with input_json_schema constrains output to the exact (including nested) structure. B relies on instruction-following without enforcement and is less reliable for nested shapes. D adds avoidable reconstruction complexity and loses the schema's guarantees. C introduces a different format with no stated advantage and abandons the schema-backed tool_use path.

scenario: Your validation-retry loop currently re-sends the entire original prompt plus a generic 'that was invalid, try again' message whenever the JSON fails validation. It still fails repeatedly on the same records and burns tokens.
stem: What single change to the retry step will most improve correction success?

options.text: On any failure, fall back to a hard-coded default object so the loop always terminates
Feed back the specific, actionable validation error (which field failed and why) and ask the model to fix exactly that
Remove the failing field from the schema so validation can no longer fail on it
Retry up to 50 times with the same generic message until it eventually passes

explanation: B gives the model the precise, actionable error so it can self-correct — the core of an effective validation-retry loop. D repeats an uninformative message; without specifics the model keeps making the same mistake. A silently substitutes fabricated defaults, masking errors. C weakens the schema to hide the problem, sacrificing the data contract rather than fixing the output.

scenario: Your team ships an MCP server with two tools: lookup_customer and lookup_account. In production, Claude frequently calls the wrong one — it pulls account records when the user asked about a customer profile. The names are short and the input schemas are nearly identical (both take an ID string). An engineer proposes renaming them to lookup_customer_v2 and lookup_account_v2.
stem: What is the most effective fix to get Claude to pick the right tool?

options.text: Merge both tools into a single tool that returns everything at once
Rewrite each tool's description to clearly state what it returns and when to use it versus the other tool
Rename the tools with version suffixes so they look distinct
Lower the model's temperature so it stops guessing between the two tools

explanation: The tool description is the single biggest driver of correct tool selection. When two tools are confusable, sharpening each description to say what it returns and when to use it (vs the sibling) is the highest-leverage fix. C (renaming with version suffixes) does not clarify semantics — names matter, but version suffixes add no disambiguating meaning. A (merging) is wrong because the tools serve genuinely different purposes; collapsing distinct concepts can hurt precision and over-fetch data. D (temperature) addresses sampling randomness, not the underlying ambiguity in the tool definitions, so the model still lacks the information to disambiguate.

scenario: An MCP tool book_meeting validates a start_time field. Right now, when the model passes a malformed timestamp, the tool throws an unhandled exception that crashes the request, and the agent loop halts. You want the agent to recover automatically.
stem: How should the tool handle invalid input so the agent can self-correct?

options.text: Re-raise the exception with a longer stack trace for debugging
Silently coerce any input to the current time and proceed
Return a structured error with isError set and a message like 'start_time must be ISO-8601, e.g. 2026-06-29T14:00:00Z'
Catch the exception and return an empty result so the loop continues

explanation: Tools should return structured, actionable errors (isError plus a message stating exactly how to fix the call) so the model can retry with corrected input. D silently swallows the error — the model gets no signal it did anything wrong and may loop or report success falsely. A returns a stack trace, which is noise the model cannot act on and leaks internals. B fabricates data (current time), producing a wrong booking with no error surfaced — a silent correctness bug. Only C enables a validation-retry self-correction loop.

scenario: You are building an MCP server for an internal wiki. You want Claude to be able to (1) call a search action it decides to invoke, (2) receive specific wiki pages the host application chooses to attach as context, and (3) offer the user a reusable 'summarize this page' template they can trigger by name.
stem: Which mapping of these three needs to MCP primitives is correct?

options.text: All three should be exposed as tools so the model can invoke them freely
Search = resource; wiki pages = prompt; summarize template = tool
Search = prompt; wiki pages = tool; summarize template = resource
Search = tool (model-invoked); wiki pages = resource (app-controlled); summarize template = prompt (user-invoked)

explanation: MCP's three primitives map by who controls them: tools are model-invoked actions, resources are application-controlled context data (like files/pages), and prompts are user-invoked templates. D matches each need correctly. B and C scramble the controllers. A is wrong because resources and prompts are deliberately NOT model-invoked — making everything a tool removes app and user control and floods the model's tool list, hurting selection.

scenario: A developer wants Claude Code to use a small filesystem-indexing MCP server that runs on the same laptop as the editor. There is no network service, no shared users, and the server is started as a child process of the host. A teammate suggests exposing it over streamable HTTP with an auth token instead.
stem: Which transport is the appropriate choice for this local server?

options.text: Either one is identical; the transport has no bearing on a local server
Streamable HTTP/SSE, because stdio cannot return structured tool results
stdio, since the host launches the server as a local subprocess on the same machine
Streamable HTTP/SSE, because it is always more secure than stdio

explanation: stdio is designed exactly for a local subprocess the host launches and communicates with over standard in/out — perfect for a same-machine server with no remote users. D is wrong: HTTP/SSE is not inherently more secure and adds needless network surface and auth complexity for a local process. B is false — stdio carries full structured tool results just like HTTP. A is wrong because transport choice does matter operationally (process model, network exposure, auth needs); stdio is the right, simpler fit here.

scenario: An agent has grown to 40 tools. Among them are seven near-duplicate 'search' tools (search_docs, search_files, search_wiki, search_kb, find_document, query_corpus, full_text_search) that overlap heavily in behavior. Selection accuracy has dropped: the model often picks a suboptimal search tool or alternates between them across turns.
stem: What is the best architectural response?

options.text: Consolidate the overlapping search tools into one well-described search tool (with a source/scope parameter), reducing the count and clarifying selection
Move all seven tools into a subagent so the orchestrator never sees them
Keep all seven but add 'PREFERRED' to one description so the model favors it
Add more search tools so the model always has an exact match for any query

explanation: Too many overlapping tools degrade selection; the fix is to consolidate them into one clear tool, optionally parameterizing the scope/source. A directly removes the ambiguity. C leaves seven confusable tools in the list — a label band-aid that does not reduce the disambiguation burden. D makes the core problem worse by adding even more overlapping choices. B just relocates the confusion: the subagent still faces seven near-duplicates, and isolating tools in a subagent is for context separation, not for masking a redundancy problem.

scenario: You run an orchestrator that delegates to subagents. One subagent's only job is to read logs and summarize errors. Currently every subagent inherits the full tool allowlist, which includes delete_resource, deploy_service, and rotate_credentials.
stem: How should you scope this read-only subagent's tools?

options.text: Keep destructive tools available but add a note in the prompt asking it not to use them
Remove all tools so it cannot cause harm, and have it summarize from memory only
Keep the full allowlist so it can handle unexpected follow-up tasks
Grant it only the read/query tools it needs and exclude write, deploy, and credential tools

explanation: Least-privilege scoping means each subagent gets only the tools its task requires. A read-summarize agent needs read/query tools and nothing destructive. C violates least privilege and widens blast radius. A relies on the model complying with a soft instruction — guardrails should be enforced structurally (by withholding the tools), not by hoping the model obeys. B over-corrects: stripping the read tools it legitimately needs makes it unable to do its job, since it cannot summarize logs it cannot read.

scenario: A create_ticket tool currently accepts a single free-form details string into which the model is expected to cram priority, assignee, and due date. The model frequently omits the priority or formats the date inconsistently, causing downstream parsing failures.
stem: What schema change will most improve reliability of the tool calls?

options.text: Split it into ten micro-tools, one per ticket field
Define explicit typed fields: priority as an enum, assignee as a string, due_date as an ISO-8601 date, and mark required ones as required
Keep the single details string but write a longer description telling the model to include everything
Accept any JSON object with no schema so the model has maximum flexibility

explanation: A tight JSON input schema with typed, required fields and enums constrains the model toward valid, parseable calls — the core of good tool schema design. B directly fixes the omitted-field and date-format issues. C keeps the ambiguous blob and merely hopes prose compensates; the model still has no structural guarantee. D removes the schema entirely, maximizing malformed input. A fragments one logical action into ten tools, exploding the tool count and forcing many round-trips — worse selection and worse ergonomics.

scenario: Your host app already knows which three contract PDFs are relevant to the current user session and wants Claude to have their contents as grounding context. An engineer is about to implement this as a tool get_contract(id) that the model must call three times to pull each document.
stem: What is the more appropriate MCP design for supplying these known documents?

options.text: Inline all three PDFs into the tool's description so they are always present
Expose the contracts as prompts so the user triggers them
Keep get_contract as a tool because only tools can carry document text
Expose the contracts as resources the application attaches to context, since the app already controls which documents are relevant

explanation: Resources are application-controlled context data (like files) — exactly the right primitive when the host already knows which documents matter and wants to attach them. D avoids forcing the model to discover and call a tool repeatedly for data the app already selected. C is false: resources carry document content too; tools are not the only way. B misuses prompts, which are user-invoked templates, not app-selected data. A is an anti-pattern: tool descriptions should describe usage, not embed large documents — that bloats every request and pollutes selection context.

scenario: You are deploying a remote MCP server over HTTP that wraps a partner billing API. The server needs an API key to reach the partner. A junior engineer's draft puts the key string inside the tool's description field so 'the model always has it,' and returns the full raw API response including internal tokens.
stem: What is the correct security posture for this server?

options.text: Return the entire raw response including internal tokens so the model has full context
Disable authentication entirely since MCP transport is already secure
Embed the API key in the description so the model can authenticate itself
Keep credentials server-side and out of tool descriptions and outputs; scope access to least privilege and return only the needed fields

explanation: Credentials must stay server-side, never in tool descriptions or returned data, and access should be least-privilege with only necessary fields returned. D is the correct posture. C leaks the secret into model-visible text (and likely logs/transcripts) — a credential exposure. A returns internal tokens to the model, another leak and an injection risk. B is wrong: the transport being networked does not remove the need to authenticate to the partner API or to the server itself; remote transports make auth more important, not optional.

scenario: You require strict JSON output from Claude to drive a downstream pipeline. You define a tool with an input_json_schema and the model returns a tool_use block. Occasionally the returned input is missing a required field. The current code just passes whatever comes back to the pipeline, which then breaks.
stem: What is the best way to make the structured output reliable?

options.text: Increase max_tokens so the model has room to include all fields
Validate the tool_use input against the schema and, on failure, feed the specific validation error back and ask the model to correct it
Switch to asking for JSON in plain prose and regex-parse the assistant text
Accept partial output and let the pipeline fill missing fields with defaults silently

explanation: The recommended pattern for structured output is tool_use plus a validation-retry loop: validate the returned input, and on failure feed the exact error back so the model can fix it. B implements this. C abandons the schema-backed tool_use mechanism for fragile regex parsing of prose. D masks errors with silent defaults, producing wrong data downstream with no signal. A misdiagnoses the cause — missing a required field is not a length/truncation problem, so more tokens does not guarantee schema-valid output.

scenario: A teammate new to MCP asks you to explain the basic architecture before they build their first server. They are unsure what role their code plays versus what Claude's host application plays.
stem: Which statement correctly describes MCP's architecture?

options.text: MCP is a proprietary Anthropic-only protocol where the model hosts the server
MCP is a peer-to-peer protocol with no distinction between client and server
MCP is an open standard using a client-server model; the host's MCP client connects to MCP servers that expose tools, resources, and prompts
MCP servers call into the model directly to generate completions on demand

explanation: MCP is an open standard with a client-server architecture: the host application's MCP client connects to servers that expose the three primitives (tools, resources, prompts). C is correct. A is wrong on two counts — MCP is an open standard, not proprietary, and the model does not host the server. B is wrong: MCP explicitly distinguishes client and server roles. D inverts the relationship — the client/host drives the model; servers expose capabilities and do not call the model to generate completions.

scenario: A tool named process takes an action string ('refund', 'cancel', 'upgrade', 'export') and a vague description: 'Processes the request.' The model often calls it with the wrong action or invents actions that are not supported, and support staff cannot tell from logs what each call did.
stem: Which redesign best improves correct usage and observability?

options.text: Replace the catch-all with clearly named, well-described tools (or a strict action enum) so each capability is unambiguous and its description states exactly when to use it
Keep the name 'process' but raise the model to a more capable tier so it guesses better
Add a free-text 'notes' field so the model can explain what it intended
Document the supported actions only in external wiki pages the model cannot see

explanation: Clear, unambiguous names plus precise descriptions are what drive correct selection; a vague catch-all with a free-form action invites invented actions and opaque logs. A fixes both: distinct named tools (or at minimum a strict enum) constrain inputs and make logs self-describing. B throws a more capable model at a definitional problem instead of fixing the ambiguous interface. C lets the model narrate intent but does nothing to prevent wrong/invented actions. D puts the guidance where the model cannot read it — the description, which the model actually sees, must carry the usage rules.

scenario: An agent already uses several built-in tools provided by the host plus a handful of custom MCP tools. The team is tempted to also register every internal microservice (about 60 endpoints) as individual tools 'so the agent can do anything,' even though most are rarely needed.
stem: What is the soundest approach to which tools to expose?

options.text: Stop using the host's built-in tools so there is room for the 60 custom ones
Register all 60 but hide them behind generic names to keep the list short
Register all 60 endpoints so the agent never lacks a capability
Expose only the tools the agent's tasks actually require; registering all 60 would bloat the tool list and degrade selection

explanation: Tool selection degrades as the tool list grows and as overlap increases, so you expose only what the task needs (least privilege plus consolidation). D is correct. C floods the model with 60 mostly-irrelevant tools, hurting selection accuracy. B keeps all 60 (the real problem) and makes them worse by stripping the descriptive names the model relies on to choose. A discards useful built-in tools for no benefit — the issue is the 60 unnecessary custom tools, not the built-ins.

scenario: Three separate teams each built their own slightly different 'send_email' integration inside their own agents. Maintenance is painful, behaviors diverge, and onboarding a new client app means re-implementing email again. Leadership wants one reliable way to send email across all current and future agents.
stem: What approach best supports reuse and consistency?

options.text: Expose email as a resource so the host attaches it to context
Have each agent keep its own email tool but agree on a shared naming convention
Build one well-designed MCP email server with clear tools and structured errors, then distribute it so every client connects to the same server
Copy the best team's email code into each agent's repo so they all start identical

explanation: MCP's value here is build-once, distribute-many: a single well-designed server with clear tool definitions and structured errors can be reused by every current and future client, ensuring consistent behavior. C is correct. D duplicates code into three repos, so they immediately drift again and onboarding still means copying. B standardizes only names while keeping three divergent implementations — the maintenance and consistency problem remains. A misuses the resource primitive: sending email is a model-invoked action (a tool), not application-controlled context data.

scenario: Your agent has a delete_records tool. A soft instruction in the system prompt tells Claude to never delete production rows, but in rare runs the model still calls delete_records against the prod table. Compliance requires that production deletes be impossible via the agent, regardless of what the model decides.
stem: What is the most reliable way to enforce this guardrail?

options.text: Strengthen the system prompt wording and add three few-shot examples of refusing prod deletes
Lower the temperature so the model is less likely to choose the delete tool
Add a PreToolUse hook that inspects the delete_records call and blocks it (exit code 2) when it targets production, feeding the reason back to the model
Switch to a more capable model tier so it follows the instruction more consistently

explanation: Hooks are deterministic, code-enforced callbacks at lifecycle events (here PreToolUse); a hook can inspect the call and block it with exit code 2, feeding the reason back to Claude — enforcement in code rather than hoping the model complies. C is correct and meets a hard compliance requirement. A, B, and D all reduce probability but remain probabilistic: prompt wording, temperature, and model tier can all still let a prod delete through, so none of them make it impossible. When the requirement is a hard guarantee, you enforce it structurally with a hook, not by tuning the model.

scenario: Your team builds a contract-review assistant. Each request includes a 40-page contract plus a short list of three hard compliance rules the answer must obey (e.g., 'never approve clauses lacking a liability cap'). Early testing shows the model frequently ignores the compliance rules when the contract is long, even though the rules are clearly stated somewhere in the prompt.
stem: Where should you place the three compliance rules in the prompt to maximize the chance the model follows them?

options.text: In the middle of the contract text so they sit next to the relevant clauses
At an edge of the context — e.g., in the system prompt at the start and/or restated right before the query at the end
Spread one rule at the top, one in the exact middle, and one at the bottom to cover all positions
Omit them from the prompt and rely on the model's general knowledge of compliance

explanation: Models exhibit the 'lost in the middle' effect — they attend best to the start and end of long context and worst to the middle. Placing critical instructions at an edge (system prompt at the start and/or restated just before the query at the end) maximizes adherence. A and C deliberately bury rules in the weak middle position. D removes the rules entirely, guaranteeing inconsistent compliance and relying on generic knowledge instead of the team's specific policy.

scenario: You must classify 2 million archived support tickets into 12 categories for an analytics dashboard. The dashboard is refreshed weekly and nobody is waiting on the results in real time. Cost is the dominant concern; a multi-hour turnaround is perfectly acceptable.
stem: Which approach best fits this workload?

options.text: Use the synchronous Messages API with high concurrency to finish as fast as possible
Switch to Opus on the synchronous API to reduce the number of retries
Use prompt caching alone on the synchronous API to make the job free
Use the Batch API to process the tickets asynchronously at roughly half the cost

explanation: The Batch API is asynchronous and ~50% cheaper, ideal for bulk, non-latency-sensitive jobs like this. A optimizes latency the task doesn't need while paying full price. C misstates caching (reads are ~10% of base input cost, not free, and caching alone doesn't make a job asynchronous or half-price). B picks the most expensive model for simple high-volume classification where a Haiku-class model would be cheaper and Batch is the real cost lever.

scenario: You run a developer-docs search that must answer both conceptual questions ('how does retry backoff work?') and exact-token lookups ('what does error code E_4471 mean?' or 'the flag --no-verify-ssl'). A pure embedding (semantic) retriever does well on concepts but frequently misses the exact error codes and CLI flags.
