Leave it in the middle but bold it and add several exclamation points
Move the critical rule to the exact middle so it is equidistant from both ends
Duplicate the entire CLAUDE.md three times so the rule appears more often overall

explanation: Models exhibit 'lost in the middle': they attend best to the beginning and end of long context and worst to the middle. The remedy is to place the most important instructions at the edges, so moving the critical rule to the start (and optionally restating it at the end) maximizes the chance it is honored, while less critical material can tolerate the middle. B relies on formatting emphasis, which does not overcome the positional attention weakness. D bloats context and still leaves no guarantee about position; it wastes the budget and can worsen attention overall. C is the worst placement possible, putting the most important rule exactly where attention is weakest.

scenario: Two recurring jobs are up for automation. Job 1: on every merge to main, run the same fixed sequence — lint, run tests, build, then post the result to Slack. The steps never vary. Job 2: triage an incoming bug report of unknown shape, which may require reading arbitrary files, reproducing, and deciding among many possible next steps that cannot be enumerated in advance.
stem: How should each job be built?

options.text: Both as fully autonomous agents, since agents are more capable than workflows
Job 1 as a deterministic workflow (predefined code path); Job 2 as an agent that dynamically directs its own tool use
Job 1 as an agent for flexibility; Job 2 as a fixed workflow to keep it predictable
Both as deterministic workflows, since determinism is always safer and cheaper

explanation: Workflows are predefined code paths: deterministic, predictable, and cheaper, and they are the right choice when the steps are fixed and known, exactly like Job 1's lint/test/build/notify sequence. Agents let the model dynamically direct its own process and tool use; that flexibility is what an open-ended task of unknown shape like Job 2 requires. The guidance is to prefer the simplest thing that works and add agentic autonomy only when the task genuinely needs dynamic decisioning. B matches each job to the right tool. A over-applies agents to a fixed sequence, paying for nondeterminism with no benefit. D forces a deterministic path onto a task that cannot be fully enumerated, so it will fail on novel cases. C inverts both assignments.

scenario: The team wants two distinct safety behaviors. First, when a developer explores a risky multi-file change interactively, they want Claude to research and propose a plan first without editing any files until the human approves. Second, in CI they want Claude to run non-interactively on each PR, with its output piped as JSON into a downstream script, and no interactive prompts.
stem: Which two Claude Code capabilities map to these requirements?

options.text: Use a PreToolUse hook for the interactive planning flow, and Plan mode in CI
Use headless mode for both flows, since it is non-interactive and therefore safe
Use a custom slash command for planning, and a subagent for the CI flow because subagents cannot edit files
Use Plan mode for the read-only research/plan-before-editing flow, and headless mode (claude -p "..." --output-format json) for the non-interactive CI flow

explanation: Plan mode is specifically the read-only research-and-plan-before-editing capability: Claude investigates and proposes a plan without making edits until the human approves, which is exactly the first requirement. Headless/non-interactive mode is invoked with claude -p "prompt" for CI/CD and scripting, and supports --output-format json so output can be piped to a downstream script, matching the second requirement. A miscasts a hook (a deterministic guardrail callback, not a planning UX) and puts interactive Plan mode into non-interactive CI. B ignores that the interactive planning flow needs Plan mode's read-only approval gate, not headless execution. C is wrong on facts: planning is Plan mode, not a slash command, and subagents are not defined by an inability to edit files; the CI requirement is about non-interactive headless execution.

topic: MCP tool design and structured errors
scenario: The team builds an internal MCP server exposing a deploy-status tool to Claude Code. When a developer passes an environment name that does not exist, the current implementation throws an unhandled exception, and Claude often gives up or hallucinates a status. They also have three nearly identical tools (get_deploy, fetch_deploy, deploy_lookup) that confuse tool selection, and the descriptions are vague.
stem: Which set of changes best improves both reliability and correct tool selection?

options.text: Make the tool always return success with an empty status so Claude never sees an error and the flow never stops
Add more example tools so the model has more options to choose from, and leave error handling unchanged
Keep throwing exceptions but wrap the whole MCP server in a retry loop so transient and permanent failures both retry
Return a structured error (isError plus an actionable message listing valid environments), consolidate the three overlapping tools into one, and write a clear unambiguous name and description

explanation: Good MCP tool design returns structured errors (isError plus an actionable message) so the model can self-correct rather than receiving an exception it cannot reason about; listing the valid environments gives Claude what it needs to fix the call. Overlapping tools should be consolidated because too many similar tools degrade selection, and the description is the single biggest driver of correct tool selection, so it must be clear and unambiguous. D does all three. C retries permanent errors (an invalid environment will never succeed on retry) and never gives the model an actionable message. B makes selection worse by adding more confusable options and leaves the unhandled-exception problem in place. A masks real failures by faking success, which violates the principle of propagating errors explicitly and will cause Claude to report or act on a nonexistent status.

scenario: Your team wants to add an automated code-quality pass to a GitHub Actions workflow. A job should invoke Claude Code on the checked-out repo, have it review the diff, and then the shell script needs to programmatically read Claude's verdict to decide whether to fail the job. There is no human at a terminal during the run.
stem: What is the correct way to invoke Claude Code in this CI job so the script can reliably parse the result?

options.text: Call the raw Messages API with curl instead, since Claude Code cannot run without a TTY
Run `claude -p "<prompt>" --output-format json` and parse the JSON (e.g. the `.result` field) with `jq`
Run `claude -p "<prompt>"` and rely on the model to print a machine-readable line you grep for
Run `claude` interactively and screen-scrape the TUI output from the job log

explanation: Headless/non-interactive mode is exactly `claude -p` (print mode), and `--output-format json` produces a structured payload (including `.result`, `session_id`, and cost fields) that a script can parse deterministically with jq. B is correct. D is wrong because the interactive TUI requires a terminal and its output is not a stable parsing contract — that is the whole reason `-p` exists. C is a plausible mistake: `-p` alone returns free-form text, and grepping for a model-emitted token is brittle because the model's phrasing varies; the JSON format gives you a guaranteed schema. A is a misconception — Claude Code runs fine headless via `-p` and is the intended CI entry point; dropping to raw curl throws away the agentic loop and tooling Claude Code provides.

scenario: You want a deterministic guardrail in CI: before Claude is allowed to run any Bash command, a PreToolUse hook must reject commands matching a denylist (e.g. `rm -rf`, `curl | sh`). When a command is blocked, you want Claude to receive a clear explanation so it can choose a safer alternative rather than the run just dying.
stem: How should the PreToolUse hook script signal a block so the message is fed back to Claude?

options.text: Write the explanation to stdout and exit 0
Write the explanation to stderr and exit 2
Write the explanation to stderr and exit 1
Exit 2 with no output, and let Claude infer why the command failed

explanation: For Claude Code hooks, exit code 2 is the blocking signal, and the text written to stderr is fed back to Claude as the reason — so the model can self-correct. B is correct. A is wrong because exit 0 means no-decision (the normal permission flow proceeds), and on exit 0 stdout is interpreted as JSON-mode structured control, not a free-text block. C is the classic mistake: a non-zero, non-2 exit code is a *non-blocking* error — stderr is surfaced but execution continues, so the dangerous command would not actually be blocked. D blocks correctly but wastes the channel: with no stderr message Claude gets no actionable reason and cannot intelligently pick a safer path, defeating the design goal of feeding feedback back to the model.

scenario: Your `claude -p` security-review job passes on your laptop but behaves inconsistently across teammates' branches and the CI runner — sometimes loading a teammate's personal hooks, sometimes picking up an MCP server declared in the repo's `.mcp.json`, sometimes not. You need the job to produce the same behavior on every machine using only the flags you pass explicitly.
stem: What is the best way to make the headless run reproducible and independent of ambient local configuration?

options.text: Commit everyone's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` into the repo so all machines share the same user memory
Delete the repo's `.mcp.json` and `.claude/` directory before each run
Pin the model with `--model` and assume that makes runs deterministic
Add `--bare` so the run skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and CLAUDE.md, using only explicitly passed flags

explanation: Plain `claude -p` loads the same ambient context an interactive session would (user/project CLAUDE.md, hooks, MCP servers, skills, plugins), which varies per machine. `--bare` is the documented CI/scripting mode precisely because it skips that auto-discovery and uses only flags you pass explicitly, so a teammate's `~/.claude` hook or the project's `.mcp.json` won't load — the same result on every machine. D is correct. A is wrong and harmful: user-level memory is per-person and not meant to be committed; this couples machines rather than isolating the run, and it still wouldn't stop ambient hooks/MCP from loading. B is a brittle hack that deletes shared, intended project config yet still doesn't stop user-level (`~/.claude`) hooks/MCP from loading. C confuses concerns: pinning the model is good hygiene but does not address ambient config loading, and LLM output is not bit-deterministic anyway, so `--model` alone does not solve the variance described.

scenario: A platform team is designing the CI gate. Most PRs just need a fixed sequence: run the linter, run tests, and have Claude review the diff against a checklist, then pass/fail. A small minority of PRs touch a sprawling legacy module where the right investigation path is genuinely open-ended and can't be scripted in advance.
stem: What is the most appropriate design for the bulk of PRs versus the exceptional ones?

options.text: Use a pure scripted workflow for all PRs and never invoke the model's own decisioning
Hand every PR to a hub-and-spoke team of subagents regardless of complexity
Use a deterministic workflow (scripted steps) for the common fixed-sequence PRs, and reserve agentic autonomy only for the open-ended legacy cases
Use a single fully-autonomous agent for every PR so behavior is uniform across the pipeline

explanation: The guidance is to prefer the simplest thing that works: workflows (predefined code paths) are deterministic, predictable, and cheaper, so they fit the fixed-sequence majority; agentic autonomy — where the model dynamically directs its own tool use — should be added only where the task genuinely needs dynamic decisioning, like the open-ended legacy module. C matches both halves. D over-applies autonomy: making every PR fully agentic adds cost, nondeterminism, and gating headaches for tasks that are just a fixed sequence. A under-applies the model: the common path still includes a checklist *review* that benefits from the model, and 'never invoke decisioning' ignores the legacy cases that truly need it. B is the over-engineering trap — multi-agent orchestration for trivial fixed-sequence checks is unjustified complexity.

scenario: Inside the CI job, after the review, a downstream step needs a strict machine-readable verdict object: `{ "verdict": "pass"|"fail", "blocking_issues": [...], "severity": "low"|"med"|"high" }`. Occasionally the model returns prose around the JSON or a near-miss schema, which breaks the parser and fails the pipeline spuriously.
stem: What is the most reliable way to obtain conformant structured output for the gate?

options.text: Parse the prose with a regex that extracts the first `{...}` block
Define a tool with an input JSON schema for the verdict, have the model emit a tool_use block, then validate and retry by feeding the validation error back on failure
Append 'Return only JSON, no other text' to the prompt and trust it every time
Raise temperature so the model explores more formats until one parses

explanation: The recommended pattern for structured output is tool_use with an input_json_schema (the tool_use input is constrained to conform to the schema), backed by a validation-retry loop: validate the JSON, and on failure feed the specific error back and ask for correction. B captures both the schema-constrained generation and the self-correcting loop. C is a weaker version of the right idea — a plain instruction helps but gives no schema enforcement and no recovery path when it slips, which is exactly the failure being described. D is backwards: higher temperature increases output variance, making schema drift worse, not better. A treats the symptom with a brittle regex that still fails on the near-miss schemas and missing fields that the validation step is meant to catch.

scenario: Your CI runs on every push across dozens of repos, hundreds of times a day. One step is a cheap, high-volume, well-defined classification: label each changed file as 'docs', 'test', 'config', or 'source'. A separate, rare step does deep architectural reasoning about a risky refactor. Cost is a real concern given the volume.
stem: How should you assign Claude models across these two steps?

options.text: Use one model for everything to keep the pipeline simple, regardless of step
Use a Haiku-class model for the high-volume file classification and an Opus-class model for the rare deep architectural reasoning
Use Sonnet for the classification and Haiku for the deep architectural reasoning
Use Opus for both steps to maximize quality everywhere

explanation: Match the model to the task: Haiku is the fast/cheap choice for high-volume, well-defined classification/extraction, while Opus is reserved for the hardest reasoning. B aligns each step with the right tier and controls cost at the volume described. D wastes money — running Opus on hundreds of trivial classifications a day is exactly the misallocation Haiku exists to avoid. C inverts the tiers: putting the weaker/cheaper model on the hard reasoning and a pricier one on trivial labeling is the worst of both. A ignores that the two steps have very different cost/quality profiles; 'one model for simplicity' sacrifices either quality on the hard step or cost on the high-volume step.

scenario: A CI 'review' job orchestrates several independent checks in parallel: a security scan, a test-coverage analysis, and a dependency-license audit — each over a large set of files. Run naively in one context, the combined file dumps blow past a sane token budget and the orchestrator's reasoning degrades as unrelated material piles up.
stem: What is the best architecture to keep each check focused while controlling the orchestrator's context?

options.text: Progressively summarize the file contents into one shrinking blob and run all checks against that summary
Concatenate every file and all three task instructions into one giant prompt so the model sees the full picture at once
Use an orchestrator that delegates each check to a subagent in its own isolated context window; each subagent returns only its result, not its full transcript
Run all three checks in one context but instruct the model to ignore the parts it isn't currently working on

explanation: Subagents run in isolated context windows, which prevents one check's bulky material from polluting the orchestrator or the sibling checks; in hub-and-spoke each subagent returns only its result, not its transcript, keeping the orchestrator's context lean. C is correct. B is the context-stuffing anti-pattern: it inflates tokens and triggers 'lost in the middle' degradation as unrelated content competes for attention. D relies on the model to self-partition attention, which it cannot do reliably — the irrelevant tokens still consume budget and degrade focus. A is dangerous for these checks: progressive summarization loses detail and provenance, so a security scan or license audit over a lossy summary can miss the exact lines/strings it must inspect.

scenario: Your headless review job connects to an internal MCP server. The same server happens to expose tools to read repo files, post PR comments, AND deploy to production. In CI you only want Claude to read files and post review comments — never deploy. You also keep getting wrong-tool selection because several read tools overlap in purpose.
stem: What is the best way to configure tool access for this job?

options.text: Keep all tools available but set a low temperature so the model is less likely to pick deploy
Scope the job to least privilege — only the read and comment tools — and consolidate the overlapping read tools so selection is unambiguous
Expose all server tools and add a sentence in the prompt telling Claude not to deploy
Remove the MCP server entirely and have Claude shell out to the deploy CLI only when it judges it safe

explanation: Two MCP best practices apply: scope tool access to least privilege (don't expose deploy in a review job), and consolidate overlapping tools because too many similar tools degrades selection. B does both. C relies on prompt-level compliance to withhold a powerful capability — guardrails should be enforced structurally, not by hoping the model obeys an instruction. A misunderstands temperature: it affects sampling randomness, not capability scoping, and a destructive tool should simply not be reachable. D is worse on every axis: it removes the legitimate read/comment tools you need and hands the model a *more* direct, less governed path to deploy.

scenario: The CI agent applies a suggested fix and then needs to decide pass/fail. Sometimes a tool call (e.g. running the test suite) errors out or returns ambiguous output, and the agent currently treats a missing failure as success and exits 0 — occasionally green-lighting a build whose tests never actually ran.
stem: What change best hardens the gate's reliability?

options.text: Trust the model's self-assessment that the build is fine, since it has full context
Always exit 0 from the job and surface problems only in a human-read log
Add an explicit verify step that checks the tool output, and propagate errors as a non-zero exit instead of silently treating absence-of-failure as success
Swallow tool errors and retry indefinitely until something returns success

explanation: The agentic loop's final phase is 'verify the work,' and reliability guidance says to verify tool outputs and propagate errors explicitly rather than swallowing them. C does both: it confirms the tests actually ran and produced a real pass before signaling success, and it fails closed on error. A over-trusts the model: self-assessment is not verification, and the described bug is precisely the agent assuming success without evidence. D hides failures and can loop forever, never surfacing the real problem to the gate. B defeats the purpose of a CI gate — always exiting 0 means the pipeline never actually blocks bad builds, just logs them for a human who may never look.

scenario: A CI run executes inside a repo that has a committed `./CLAUDE.md` with project conventions. The runner image also has a user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` baked in by whoever built the image, and the org publishes an enterprise/managed-policy CLAUDE.md. A reviewer notices the agent following an outdated rule and asks which configuration is authoritative. Assume bare mode is NOT used.
stem: Which statement about CLAUDE.md precedence is correct for this run?

options.text: Only the project `./CLAUDE.md` is ever loaded in CI; user and enterprise files are ignored
The user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` always wins because it is loaded last
Project `./CLAUDE.md` overrides enterprise policy because it is closest to the code
All three files load and combine, and the enterprise/managed-policy CLAUDE.md is authoritative — it loads first and cannot be excluded or overridden by user or project files

explanation: In the memory hierarchy the enterprise/managed-policy CLAUDE.md loads first and is the guardrail tier that user and project files cannot exclude or override; all applicable files combine as context. D states this correctly. B is wrong on both facts: user is not the most authoritative tier and 'loaded last wins' is not how this works — managed policy outranks user. A is false: without `--bare`, a normal `-p` run does load user and enterprise/managed config (which is the very reason this reviewer is confused). C inverts the key guarantee — managed policy is specifically designed to be un-overridable by project files, so project cannot win over enterprise. (Note: across the user vs. project tiers the files are additive context rather than strictly ranked, but that does not rescue B, A, or C — only the enterprise-supremacy framing in D is correct.)

scenario: Your team is building a pipeline that extracts invoice fields (vendor, invoice_number, line_items, total) from thousands of OCR'd PDFs using the Claude Messages API. A junior engineer's prototype asks the model in prose to 'reply with JSON only' and then runs json.loads() on the raw text. In production this breaks intermittently: the model sometimes wraps JSON in prose, sometimes emits markdown code fences, and occasionally invents extra keys, so json.loads() throws.
stem: What is the most reliable way to make Claude return structured invoice data that conforms to your schema?

options.text: Keep the prose instruction but lower temperature to 0 so the model deterministically emits clean JSON
Switch from the Messages API to the Batch API, which automatically returns validated JSON objects
Define a tool whose input_json_schema describes the invoice fields and read the structured object from the returned tool_use block's input
Append 'IMPORTANT: output ONLY raw JSON, no markdown, no prose' in capital letters to force compliance

explanation: Correct: The canonical way to get schema-conformant structured output is tool_use — define a tool with an input_json_schema, and the model returns a tool_use block whose input is a structured object matching that schema, eliminating prose/markdown-wrapping problems. A is a plausible mistake: temperature 0 reduces sampling variance but does not constrain output to a schema or stop prose-wrapping. D is the naive prompt-only approach that already failed — emphatic instructions still leave the model free to add fences or extra keys. B confuses the Batch API (an asynchronous, cheaper way to run bulk jobs) with structured-output enforcement; Batch changes how/when requests run, not the output format.

scenario: After switching to tool_use with a JSON schema, about 3% of extracted invoice objects still fail downstream schema validation — usually a missing required field or a date in the wrong format because the source document was unusually messy. The pipeline currently drops these into a dead-letter queue for manual entry, but the manual backlog is growing.
stem: What is the best pattern to automatically recover most of these 3% schema-validation failures before escalating to a human?

options.text: Re-send the identical request unchanged up to five times, relying on transient model variance to eventually produce a valid object
Raise the model temperature on each retry so it explores different extractions until one happens to validate

Implement a validation-retry loop: when validation fails, feed the specific validation error back to the model and ask it to correct the invalid output, retrying a bounded number of times before escalating
Loosen the JSON schema to make the frequently-missing fields optional so validation stops failing

explanation: Correct: The recommended structured-output reliability pattern is a validation-retry loop — validate the returned JSON, and on failure feed the concrete error back to the model so it can self-correct, with a bounded retry count and human escalation as the final fallback. D is a plausible mistake that destroys data integrity: making required fields optional hides the failure rather than fixing it, so empty/incomplete invoices silently pass. B abandons determinism and treats correctness as a lottery; randomly higher temperature does not target the actual error. A is the 'just retry blindly' anti-pattern — without feeding back the error, the model has no new information and will likely repeat the same mistake.

scenario: The extraction workload is enormous and largely mechanical: pull six well-defined fields from millions of standardized purchase orders per month, where the fields appear in predictable positions. Cost is the dominant concern. A separate, much smaller stream involves messy, ambiguous contracts where the model must reason about clauses to decide which figures count as the 'total liability'. Leadership wants to keep ops simple but not waste money.
stem: How should you assign Claude model tiers across these two streams?

options.text: Use Sonnet for both streams as a universal middle ground to avoid maintaining two model configurations
Use Haiku for the high-volume standardized purchase orders and route only the ambiguous reasoning-heavy contracts to Opus
Standardize on Haiku for both streams since extraction is a single task category and Haiku is cheapest
Standardize on Opus for both streams because the most capable model minimizes extraction errors everywhere

explanation: Correct: Model choice should match task difficulty — Haiku is built for high-volume, cheap, well-defined extraction/classification, while Opus is reserved for the hardest reasoning. Splitting the streams gives the right cost/capability tradeoff. D wastes large amounts of money running the most expensive model on trivially structured documents. C is the plausible 'one task category' trap — it under-powers the genuinely ambiguous contract reasoning where a cheap model will make costly judgment errors. A's single mid-tier choice overpays for the trivial bulk (where Haiku suffices) and may still underperform Opus on the hardest clauses; the two distinct difficulty profiles justify two tiers, and config simplicity does not outweigh the cost and accuracy gap at this scale.

scenario: Every night a cron job receives a dump of 400,000 newly scanned receipts that must be field-extracted by 7am for the morning finance reconciliation. There is no user waiting on any individual response — only the whole batch matters, and it must be ready before reconciliation runs. Finance is pushing hard to cut the API bill.
stem: Which API approach best fits this nightly bulk extraction job?

options.text: Use the streaming Messages API so partial results arrive token-by-token and the bill is lower
Send each receipt as an individual synchronous Messages API call with high concurrency to finish as fast as possible
Concatenate all 400,000 receipts into one giant Messages API prompt so the whole job is a single billed request
Submit the receipts through the Message Batches API, which processes them asynchronously at roughly 50% lower cost

explanation: Correct: The Batch API is purpose-built for exactly this profile — large-volume, non-latency-sensitive jobs processed asynchronously at about 50% lower cost than standard Messages calls, which directly addresses both the overnight window and the cost pressure. B works functionally but forfeits the ~50% discount and adds rate-limit and orchestration overhead for no latency benefit anyone needs. A is a plausible confusion: streaming improves perceived latency for interactive use but does not reduce cost and does not suit a fire-and-forget batch. C is impossible and counterproductive — 400,000 receipts vastly exceed the 200K context window, and cramming many documents into one prompt degrades per-document accuracy rather than saving money.

scenario: Your extraction is accurate on clean invoices but systematically mishandles a recurring edge case: when an invoice shows a credit/refund, the 'total' is negative and parenthesized like (1,250.00), and the model keeps extracting it as a positive 1250.00. The field's tool schema already types total as a number.
stem: What is the most effective prompt-engineering change to fix this specific recurring error?

options.text: Remove the tool schema's number type so the model can return the raw string and let downstream code parse it
Add a few-shot example to the prompt showing a parenthesized-credit invoice mapped to a negative number, explicitly covering this edge case
Escalate to Opus, since a more capable model will infer the accounting convention without examples
Add 'be accurate and careful with totals' to the system prompt

explanation: Correct: A targeted few-shot example demonstrating the exact edge case (parenthesized credit -> negative number) is the prescribed way to teach the model an ambiguous convention; examples that cover edge cases are far more effective than abstract exhortations. D is the classic vague-instruction mistake — 'be careful' gives the model no concrete mapping for the parenthesis convention. A pushes the problem downstream and discards the schema's type guarantee, adding brittle string parsing instead of fixing the extraction. C is a plausible but wasteful fix: throwing a bigger model at a teachable, well-defined convention is costly and still less reliable than simply showing the rule via an example.

topic: lost in the middle / context placement
scenario: Some source documents are 40+ page master service agreements, and the field you need (the governing payment terms) can appear anywhere. You assemble one long prompt: the full document text, then your extraction instructions and the tool definition at the very end. Accuracy is noticeably worse on the longest documents, with the model sometimes ignoring instructions buried after huge documents or grabbing the wrong clause from the middle.
stem: Which change best improves reliability on these long documents?

options.text: Insert the extraction instructions into the exact middle of the document so they sit closest to the relevant clauses
Concatenate all 40 pages onto a single line to reduce token count and help the model see everything at once
Disable prompt caching, since cached prefixes are what cause the model to lose track of mid-document content
Place the long document early, keep key instructions at the start and end of the prompt, and ask the model to first quote the relevant clauses before emitting the extracted fields

explanation: Correct: Models attend best to the start and end of long context and worst to the middle ('lost in the middle'), so important instructions belong at the edges; putting the long document before the query and asking the model to quote relevant parts first is the recommended long-document pattern. A does the opposite of best practice — the middle is precisely where attention is weakest, so instructions there are most likely ignored. C misattributes the problem to caching, which only affects cost/latency of a stable prefix and has no effect on how the model attends to content. B is a plausible-sounding but false fix: collapsing whitespace does not meaningfully cut tokens or change attention dynamics and destroys structural cues the model relies on.

scenario: For high-value invoices (over $50,000) that feed an auto-payment system, a wrong 'total' could trigger an erroneous large payment. Your extraction returns the fields plus a self-reported confidence and, for low-confidence cases, the source text is genuinely ambiguous (smudged OCR). The business cannot tolerate silent errors on these high-stakes records.
stem: What is the most appropriate reliability design for these high-value, ambiguous extractions?

options.text: When confidence is low, silently fall back to the field value from a previous similar invoice so the pipeline never blocks
Discard low-confidence high-value records entirely so no risky payment can be made
Route low-confidence high-value extractions to a human-in-the-loop review queue before the payment is allowed to proceed, while auto-processing high-confidence ones
Auto-process every extraction and rely on the monthly reconciliation to catch any wrong payments after the fact

explanation: Correct: The reliability doctrine for low-confidence, high-stakes outputs is to escalate to a human — gate auto-payment behind human review for low-confidence high-value cases while letting confident cases flow through, balancing safety and throughput. D accepts silent errors on exactly the records the business said it cannot tolerate, catching mistakes only after money has moved. A invents data by substituting an unrelated invoice's value — a silent fabrication that is worse than failing loudly. B throws away legitimate business documents and creates an operational gap (unpaid high-value invoices), an overcorrection; escalation, not deletion, is the right handling.

scenario: Your extraction agent calls an internal lookup tool, validate_vendor(vendor_name), to confirm each extracted vendor against the master vendor list before writing the record. Sometimes the extracted vendor name is a near-miss ('Acme Corp.' vs canonical 'ACME Corporation'). Currently validate_vendor raises an unstructured exception on any miss, which crashes the turn and the orchestrator just logs a stack trace.
stem: How should you redesign validate_vendor's failure behavior so the agent can recover automatically?

options.text: Make validate_vendor always return success and push all mismatch handling into a separate nightly cleanup job
Keep throwing the raw exception but wrap the whole agent loop in a try/except that retries the identical call
Return a structured tool error (isError set, with an actionable message and suggested close matches) so the model can self-correct and retry with a corrected vendor name
Broaden the tool to also create new vendor records automatically whenever a name is not found, so it never reports a failure

explanation: Correct: Tools should return structured errors (isError plus an actionable, informative message — here, suggested close matches) so the model can read the error and self-correct rather than the process throwing. B preserves the unstructured throw; retrying the identical call gives the model no information to fix the name and will fail again. A hides real mismatches and defers data-quality problems, reintroducing silent errors. D violates least-privilege and conflates validation with mutation — auto-creating vendor records on every miss is dangerous (it would pollute the master list with OCR typos) and far exceeds what a read-only validation tool should do.

scenario: Every extraction request shares a large, stable preamble: a 6,000-token extraction policy, the tool definition, and a fixed set of few-shot examples. Only the per-document text at the end changes. You are running millions of requests and want to cut input-token cost with prompt caching.
stem: How should you structure the prompt to maximize prompt-cache savings?

options.text: Put the variable per-document text first and the stable preamble last, since the model reads the document before the instructions
Interleave a few document-specific tokens into the preamble to keep the cache 'warm' across different documents

Place the stable policy, tool definition, and few-shot examples first as a cacheable prefix marked with cache_control, with the variable per-document text last, so repeated requests get cache reads at about 10% of base input cost
Rely on the Batch API discount instead of caching, because caching and batching cannot be combined

explanation: Correct: Prompt caching requires a stable prefix — order content stable-to-variable, mark the stable prefix with cache_control (ephemeral), and repeated requests then read the cached prefix at roughly 10% of base input-token cost (5-minute TTL refreshed on each use). A breaks caching entirely: any variation at the front invalidates the cached prefix, so nothing downstream can be reused. B is a plausible misconception — injecting document-specific tokens into the prefix changes it per request and defeats the cache; the cache stays 'warm' by being reused unchanged, not by edits. D states a false constraint: per Anthropic's docs the Batch and prompt-caching discounts explicitly stack, so you do not have to choose one.

scenario: You want to wrap the whole extraction job in a CI pipeline: a nightly GitHub Action checks out the repo, runs the extractor over a folder of new documents, and a downstream step parses the result to update a database. No human is at a terminal, and the next step needs machine-readable output it can parse deterministically.
stem: How should you invoke Claude Code so it fits cleanly into this non-interactive CI step?

options.text: Add the extraction instructions to the project CLAUDE.md so CI automatically performs the extraction on checkout
Launch Claude Code in interactive mode and use an expect script to type the prompt and screen-scrape the TUI output
Run Claude Code in plan mode so it produces the extraction without making changes, then read the plan text as the result
Run Claude Code headless with claude -p "<prompt>" and --output-format json, then pipe the structured output into the next pipeline step

explanation: Correct: For CI/CD and scripting, Claude Code's headless/non-interactive mode (claude -p "prompt") is the intended path, and --output-format json gives machine-readable output you can pipe to the next step. B is brittle and unnecessary — driving the interactive TUI with expect and screen-scraping is exactly what headless mode exists to avoid. C misunderstands plan mode, which is a read-only research/planning mode for proposing changes, not a data-extraction output format. A misunderstands CLAUDE.md, which is passive memory/instructions that load into context; it does not by itself trigger or run any job during checkout.

scenario: Your Customer Support Resolution Agent runs on claude-sonnet-4-6 and occasionally a user asks it to do something against policy (e.g., issue a fraudulent refund). When this happens, the API call returns HTTP 200 but the content is empty or partial, and your orchestration loop crashes because it assumed completed responses always contain usable text.
stem: Which stop_reason indicates this situation and should trigger a dedicated fallback/handoff path?

options.text: max_tokens — the response was cut off mid-generation, so you should retry with a larger max_tokens budget
pause_turn — the model paused a long-running server tool, so you should resubmit the response to continue
end_turn — the model finished normally but produced no content, so you should reparse the text blocks
refusal — the model declined for safety reasons, returning HTTP 200 with empty/partial content, so you route to a refusal fallback

explanation: D is correct: the "refusal" stop_reason is a successful HTTP 200 response where Claude declined to continue, leaving content empty or partial, so your loop must detect it and route to a safe fallback or human handoff. A is wrong because max_tokens means the output was truncated by length, not declined, and content is still present. B is wrong because pause_turn relates to long-running server tool calls and is resolved by resubmitting, not by a refusal fallback. C is wrong because end_turn signals normal completion with real content, and you should never detect completion or refusals by text-parsing content blocks.

scenario: In a multi-agent research system, a sub-agent running on claude-sonnet-4-6 is mid-investigation. The orchestrator receives one response with stop_reason 'max_tokens' where the content ends with a partial tool_use block, and a separate, later response that fails with an HTTP 529 (overloaded) error.
stem: How should the orchestrator correctly handle these two distinct events?

options.text: For the 'max_tokens' case, discard the incomplete turn and re-request with a higher max_tokens (or continue the turn) since the tool_use block was truncated and cannot be executed; for the 529, retry the API call with exponential backoff as it is a transient server-side error.
Treat both events identically as turn failures and abort the sub-agent's research task, returning a partial result to the orchestrator in both cases.
For the 'max_tokens' case, attempt to parse and execute the partial tool_use input as-is and return a tool_result, then continue; for the 529, surface it to the user as a refusal.
For both cases, text-parse the content blocks to determine whether the agent intended to finish, and only retry if no concluding sentence is found.

explanation: A is correct: 'max_tokens' means generation was cut off, so a truncated tool_use is unusable and you must re-request with more room (or continue the turn) rather than treat it as a hard failure, while an HTTP 529 is a transient overloaded error that should be retried with backoff. B wrongly conflates a recoverable truncation and a retryable server error into task abortion. C is dangerous: a truncated tool_use has incomplete/invalid input JSON and must not be executed, and a 529 is a network/server error, not a 'refusal' (refusal is a stop_reason on a 200 response). D violates the rule that you never detect completion by text-parsing content—you branch on stop_reason and HTTP status, not prose.

scenario: A CI/CD pipeline runs Claude Code in headless mode (claude -p) with the web_search server tool enabled to gather release-note context. On one build, the API response comes back with stop_reason "pause_turn" mid server-tool execution, and your orchestration wrapper must decide how to continue the long-running search.
stem: What is the correct way to handle the "pause_turn" stop_reason so the server-tool run completes?

options.text: Treat pause_turn as a terminal failure, discard the partial response, and restart the entire task from the original user prompt.
Make a follow-up request that appends the returned response.content (as an assistant message) back to the conversation, letting Claude resume the in-progress server-tool turn.
Parse the partial content text for a completion marker, and if none is found, re-issue the original messages array unchanged with a higher max_tokens.
Execute the web_search yourself locally, wrap the results in a tool_result block, and send that back as the next user turn.

explanation: B is correct: pause_turn signals a paused long-running (server-tool) turn, and you resume it by sending the response.content back as an assistant message in a follow-up request so Claude continues where it left off. A is wrong because restarting throws away valid progress and is unnecessary—pause_turn is resumable, not a failure. C is wrong because you must never detect completion by text-parsing content, and re-sending the original messages restarts rather than resumes the turn. D is wrong because web_search is a server tool that Anthropic executes; you do not run it locally or return a tool_result for it.

scenario: You are building an autonomous code-fixing agent on claude-sonnet-4-6 that loops: send messages, parse any tool_use blocks, run the requested edits/tests as client tools, append tool_result, and repeat. In a production incident the loop ran 200+ times on one ticket, burning budget, because the agent kept emitting tool calls and your driver never decided to stop.
stem: What is the most robust way to make this tool_use loop terminate correctly and safely?

options.text: After each response, scan the assistant's text content for phrases like "all tests pass" or "task complete" and break the loop when one is found.
Set tool_choice to "any" so Claude is forced to keep acting, and rely on the model eventually choosing to stop calling tools on its own.

Continue the loop only while stop_reason == "tool_use", break immediately on end_turn/refusal/max_tokens/model_context_window_exceeded, and additionally enforce a hard max-iteration cap that aborts the loop regardless of stop_reason.
Wrap the whole loop in a try/except and treat any thrown API error as the natural completion signal, since a finished task stops producing new work and the next call will error out.

explanation: C is correct: stop_reason is the authoritative control signal — keep looping while it is "tool_use", and terminate on end_turn (Claude is done), refusal, max_tokens, or model_context_window_exceeded; a hard iteration cap is still needed as a fail-safe against pathological loops. A is the anti-pattern the prompt warns against: text-parsing for "done" is brittle because wording varies, a refusal returns HTTP 200 with empty/partial content, and natural completion is signaled by end_turn, not prose. B forces tool calls with tool_choice "any", which actively prevents the model from ever emitting end_turn, so the loop can never terminate normally. D conflates stop_reason (a normal HTTP 200 field) with API errors — a completed task returns end_turn without throwing, so waiting for an exception is incorrect and would mask real failures.

scenario: Your pipeline ingests 5,000 customer-support transcripts. Each transcript must be (1) split into and extracted across four distinct independent fields — sentiment, product mentioned, resolution status, and refund amount — and (2) given a final escalation label that has been unreliable, where a single model pass disagrees with QA reviewers ~15% of the time.
stem: How should you apply parallelization patterns to this job?

options.text: Use sectioning for the four independent extraction fields by running each as a separate focused subtask, and use voting on the escalation label by running the same labeling prompt multiple times and aggregating the results.
Use voting for all four extraction fields by running each field's prompt N times, and use sectioning to split the escalation label into independent sub-labels.
Use sectioning for everything, splitting both the four fields and the escalation label into separate concurrent subtasks for maximum throughput.
Use voting for everything, running the entire combined extraction-and-labeling prompt N times and taking the majority output across all fields at once.

explanation: A correctly maps the two patterns: sectioning splits genuinely independent subtasks (the four distinct fields) to run in parallel, while voting runs the same task multiple times to boost reliability on the unreliable escalation label. B inverts both: voting wastes calls on already-reliable independent fields and sectioning cannot split a single atomic label into independent parts. C ignores the reliability problem — sectioning a low-agreement label does not improve its accuracy. D conflates patterns by voting on a whole combined prompt, which both loses the focus benefit of sectioning and produces incoherent majority votes across heterogeneous fields.

scenario: Your team uses Claude Code to generate SQL migration scripts that must pass a strict checklist: idempotent, reversible with a down-migration, and no destructive DROPs without an explicit guard. Draft quality from a single generation varies widely — some drafts are perfect, others miss the reversibility requirement entirely — but the quality bar is explicit and machine-checkable.
stem: Which orchestration pattern best fits this requirement, and why?

options.text: Prompt chaining: split generation into fixed sub-steps (schema diff, then DDL, then rollback), since decomposing the task into a static pipeline removes all quality variance.

Evaluator-optimizer: have one call generate the migration, a second call critique it against the explicit checklist, and loop refine→re-critique until it passes, because the quality bar is well-defined but individual draft quality is inconsistent.
Single-shot generation with output_config json_schema constrained decoding, since enforcing a JSON structure guarantees the migration meets the idempotency and reversibility rules.
Parallel sampling: generate five drafts concurrently and have the orchestrator pick the longest one, since more output usually correlates with completeness on migrations.

explanation: B is correct: the evaluator-optimizer (generate→critique→refine) loop is the documented fit when an explicit, checkable quality bar exists but draft quality is variable — the evaluator gives actionable feedback against the checklist and the optimizer revises until it passes. A is wrong because prompt chaining decomposes a task into fixed steps but provides no feedback loop to catch and fix variable quality, so a draft missing reversibility still ships. C is wrong because json_schema constrained decoding only enforces output *shape/syntax*, not semantic correctness like idempotency or guarded DROPs. D is wrong because picking by length is not a real quality signal and parallel sampling without an evaluator never checks the output against the actual bar.

scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. You want a specialized 'citation-checker' subagent that only verifies factual claims against fetched sources, restricted to read-only tooling, and you want your orchestrator to delegate to it on demand.
stem: What is the correct way to define this specialized subagent and have the orchestrator invoke it?

options.text: Skip an AgentDefinition entirely and instead instruct the orchestrator in its system prompt to 'pretend to be a citation checker,' relying on the model to roleplay the subagent with the same full tool set.
Define the subagent by setting prefill on the orchestrator's assistant turn so its output is forced into citation-check formatting, then text-parse the response to detect when checking is done.

Create an AgentDefinition with a description (when to use it), a focused prompt, and a scoped tools list (e.g., only web_fetch/web_search), register it, and let the orchestrator delegate to it through the Agent tool.
Define the subagent as an MCP server exposed over a WebSocket transport so the orchestrator connects to it as a separate citation-checking process.

explanation: C is correct: the Agent SDK's AgentDefinition primitive specifies a description (for delegation routing), a prompt, and a scoped tools list, and the orchestrator invokes it via the built-in Agent tool — giving true isolation and least-privilege tooling. A is wrong because roleplay in one context provides no tool scoping or real subagent isolation. B is wrong because assistant prefilling is removed on 4.6+ (returns HTTP 400), and completion must be detected via stop_reason, never by text-parsing content. D is wrong because WebSocket is not a valid MCP transport (only stdio and Streamable HTTP/SSE are), and an MCP server is unnecessary for defining an in-SDK subagent.

scenario: A multi-agent research system spins up a lead orchestrator running claude-opus-4-8 that issues three parallel tool calls — each a 'spawn_research_subagent' tool_use with a distinct id — to investigate competing hypotheses. Each subagent runs its own Claude conversation and may itself emit multiple message turns and tool calls before returning findings, and the lead must synthesize the three result streams without conflating them.
stem: How should the lead correctly attribute each incoming subagent message to the originating spawn so it can synthesize the parallel results cleanly?

options.text: Stamp every subagent's emitted messages with the parent_tool_use_id equal to the lead's spawning tool_use id, then group and synthesize the streams by matching parent_tool_use_id back to each original spawn_research_subagent call.
Concatenate all subagent outputs into a single ordered transcript and rely on the lead to text-parse headings and section breaks to determine which finding came from which hypothesis.
Detect when each subagent has finished by scanning its final text block for a completion phrase, then merge whichever results arrived before the others as authoritative.
Return all three subagent results as text blocks placed immediately after the spawn tool_result blocks in the same lead turn, letting positional order encode attribution.

explanation: A is correct: parent_tool_use_id links each subagent's messages back to the specific spawning tool_use id, giving the lead a deterministic key to group parallel streams and synthesize without conflation. B is wrong because attribution must come from structured ids, not brittle text-parsing of headings. C is wrong because completion must be read from stop_reason (end_turn/tool_use/etc.), never by scanning content for a phrase, and arrival order has no bearing on authority. D is wrong because you must never place text blocks after tool_result blocks in the same turn, and positional ordering is not a reliable attribution mechanism for parallel results.

scenario: A platform team wants Claude to answer developer questions about their internal monorepo by pulling from API docs and running a read-only repo-search tool. The questions are mostly single-hop lookups, and the team has a tight deadline and no observability tooling yet.
stem: Which initial architecture best fits this workload while avoiding premature agentic complexity?

options.text: Build a multi-agent orchestrator with a planner agent that delegates to retrieval and search sub-agents, so the system can scale to any future question type.

Start with a single augmented LLM call that retrieves the relevant docs and exposes the repo-search tool, returning answers in one or two tool round trips; add an autonomous loop later only if real traffic shows multi-step reasoning is needed.
Implement an open-ended autonomous loop where Claude repeatedly decides its next action, and detect completion by text-parsing the model's content for a phrase like 'final answer'.
Skip retrieval and instead fine-tune a model on the monorepo so no tools or context-gathering are required at query time.

explanation: B follows simplicity-first: most questions are single-hop, so an augmented LLM (model + retrieval + tools) handles them with a predictable one-or-two-turn tool round trip, and an autonomous loop is added only when evidence justifies it. A is premature complexity—a multi-agent orchestrator adds cost, latency, and failure modes the workload doesn't need. C is doubly wrong: it jumps to an autonomous loop prematurely and detects completion by text-parsing content instead of inspecting stop_reason (end_turn). D discards retrieval entirely for a costly fine-tune that can't keep pace with a changing repo, when grounded retrieval is the simpler, more accurate fit.

scenario: A customer support resolution agent built on claude-sonnet-4-6 autonomously triages tickets, looks up order status, and drafts replies. The team now wants it to also issue refunds, but a refund is irreversible and must require a human supervisor's approval, while all the read-only triage steps should remain fully autonomous.
stem: What is the best way to architect the human-in-the-loop approval gate for the refund action?

options.text: Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to ask the supervisor for permission before refunding, and rely on the model to pause and wait for a reply on its own.
Set tool_choice to "none" for the entire session so the model can never call any tool without a human first reviewing every step, including order lookups.

Keep read-only tools executing automatically, but when the model emits a tool_use for the issue_refund client tool, halt execution, route the requested action to a supervisor for approval, and only run the tool and return its tool_result once approved (returning is_error otherwise).
Define issue_refund as a server tool so Anthropic executes the refund, and inspect the response text after each turn to decide whether a refund was performed.

explanation: C is correct: the gate is enforced deterministically in your orchestration layer—non-sensitive tools run autonomously, but the issue_refund tool_use is intercepted before execution and only completes after human approval, with denial surfaced via is_error on the tool_result. A is wrong because prompt instructions are not enforcement; the model cannot reliably block its own actions and there is no mechanism for it to literally 'wait.' B is wrong because tool_choice "none" disables all tool calls, destroying the autonomy requirement for read-only triage steps. D is wrong because refunds are your business action (a client tool you execute), not an Anthropic server tool, and you must never detect completion by text-parsing content—use stop_reason/tool_use blocks instead.

scenario: Your internal coding agent (claude-sonnet-4-6) calls a repository-search tool that takes a single 'query' string and returns raw grep output across the whole monorepo. Claude frequently picks bad search terms, ignores which directory to search, and misreads the wall of unlabeled matches, so you keep appending more rules to the system prompt with little improvement.
stem: Following Anthropic's guidance on agent-computer interface (ACI) investment, what is the most effective way to make this tool reliable?

options.text: Redesign the tool's interface to be model-natural: split parameters into a clearly described 'pattern', an optional 'path_scope', and a 'max_results' limit, return structured results with file path, line number, and a snippet per match, and write a precise tool description with examples of good inputs.
Keep the tool signature unchanged and add several more paragraphs of system-prompt instructions explaining exactly how to phrase queries and how to interpret the raw grep output.
Set tool_choice to 'any' so the model is forced to call a tool every turn, which will make it use the search tool more consistently.
Switch the model to claude-haiku-4-5 and raise output_config.effort to 'max' so it reasons harder about which search terms to choose.

explanation: A applies Anthropic's ACI investment principle: a flaky tool is usually an interface problem, so make the inputs/outputs model-natural with well-named, well-described parameters and structured, labeled results rather than piling on prompt text. B is the anti-pattern the scenario already shows failing—stacking instructions cannot fix an interface that emits ambiguous inputs and unreadable output. C forces a tool call every turn but does nothing to improve which terms are chosen or how results are read, and it removes the model's ability to stop when no search is needed. D misuses effort and downgrades to the smaller 200K-context Haiku model; raising reasoning effort does not compensate for a poorly designed tool surface.

scenario: A claims-processing team must extract structured fields from each of 40 independent PDF documents in an uploaded batch, then produce a single consolidated JSON report that aggregates all extractions. Per-document extractions do not depend on one another, but end-to-end latency for the full batch must be minimized for an interactive review UI.
stem: Which orchestration topology best fits this workload?

options.text: A sequential pipeline where each document's extraction is fed as context into the next, accumulating results until the final document produces the consolidated report
A parallel fan-out that issues one independent extraction call per document concurrently, then a fan-in step that merges the per-document JSON results into the consolidated report
A single call that concatenates all 40 documents into one prompt and asks the model to emit every document's fields plus the merged report in one pass
A sequential pipeline driven by detecting completion of each document's extraction by text-parsing the model's output for a 'DONE' marker before proceeding

explanation: B is correct: because the per-document extractions are independent, fan-out lets all 40 run concurrently to minimize latency, and a dedicated fan-in/merge step assembles the consolidated report. A serializes independent work, adding latency for no benefit and risking context bloat as results accumulate. C forfeits parallelism, strains accuracy by overloading one context, and can approach context limits, surfacing model_context_window_exceeded. D is an anti-pattern: completion must be inferred from stop_reason (end_turn/tool_use/etc.), never by text-parsing content for a marker.

scenario: You're building a Customer Support Resolution Agent on claude-sonnet-4-6 that follows a gather→act→verify loop: it pulls order data via client tools, performs an account action (e.g., issuing a refund), then re-queries the system to confirm the action succeeded before responding to the customer. The agent currently runs indefinitely because the loop has no rigorous stopping rule, sometimes re-issuing refunds.
stem: Which approach correctly defines the termination condition so the loop stops exactly when verification passes?

options.text: After each turn, scan the model's text content for phrases like 'refund confirmed' or 'all done', and break the loop when such a completion phrase appears.
Force tool_choice:"any" on every turn so the model must keep calling tools, and terminate only when the API returns stop_reason "max_tokens".

Continue the tool round-trip while stop_reason is "tool_use"; after returning the verify-tool's tool_result, treat the loop as complete when the model responds with stop_reason "end_turn" and the verify tool_result confirmed success, otherwise loop again.
Use prefilling to seed the assistant turn with a JSON status object, then end the loop once the prefilled status field reads "verified".

explanation: C is correct: the agentic loop is driven by stop_reason — keep executing tools while stop_reason is "tool_use", and termination is the conjunction of a clean "end_turn" AND the verify tool's structured tool_result confirming success, which is the documented, reliable signal rather than guesswork. A is wrong because you must never detect completion by text-parsing content — phrasing is non-deterministic and easily spoofed. B is wrong because tool_choice:"any" forces a tool call every turn (preventing the model from ever ending), and "max_tokens" is a truncation/failure signal, not successful completion. D is wrong because assistant prefilling is REMOVED on the 4.6+ family (Sonnet 4.6 returns HTTP 400); structured output should use output_config.format or strict tool use instead.

scenario: Your CI/CD pipeline uses Claude Code in headless mode to handle two jobs: an interactive PR-triage bot that posts a fast pass/fail comment when a developer pushes, and a nightly job that synthesizes a deep cross-repo architecture review over thousands of diffs. The triage must respond within seconds, but the nightly synthesis tolerates hours of latency and your cost budget is tight.
stem: How should you orchestrate these two workloads to minimize cost without harming interactive responsiveness?

options.text: Keep the per-push triage on the synchronous Messages API for real-time latency, and submit the nightly synthesis jobs to the Batch API to capture the ~50% cost reduction on the latency-tolerant work.
Route both workloads through the Batch API so all Claude calls get the ~50% discount uniformly across the pipeline.
Keep both on the synchronous Messages API and rely on prompt caching alone to make the nightly synthesis as cheap as batching.
Run the triage on the Batch API but poll the batch result every second so it still feels real-time to developers.

explanation: A correctly maps each workload to the right surface: synchronous Messages API for the latency-critical triage and the async Batch API (~50% cheaper) for the latency-tolerant nightly synthesis. B is wrong because the Batch API is asynchronous and would destroy the seconds-level triage responsiveness. C forgoes the substantial batch discount on work that doesn't need real-time results — caching reduces repeated-prefix cost but is not a substitute for batching's per-job savings. D is wrong because polling a batch job cannot make it real-time; batch results are not guaranteed quickly and tight polling defeats the purpose.

scenario: Your Claude Code-style agent runs a long refactoring loop against claude-sonnet-4-6, accumulating tool_results from dozens of file reads and edits across many turns. On the latest API call, the response comes back with stop_reason 'model_context_window_exceeded' and no usable content.
stem: What is the correct way to recover and continue the agentic loop?

options.text: Immediately resend the exact same request unchanged, since model_context_window_exceeded is a transient server condition that clears on retry
Compact the conversation history (summarize/drop older tool_results and stale turns) to reduce input tokens, then continue the loop with the trimmed message list
Switch the call to claude-haiku-4-5 to gain a larger context window and replay the identical full message history
Add an assistant prefill block instructing Claude to ignore earlier context, then resend the request

explanation: B is correct: model_context_window_exceeded means the input exceeded the model's window, so you must reduce token count by compacting (summarizing or pruning older tool_results/turns) before continuing — retrying the identical payload will only overflow again. A is wrong because it is not a transient error and resending the same request reproduces it. C is wrong because Haiku 4.5 has a 200K window — smaller than Sonnet's 1M default — so it would overflow sooner, not later. D is wrong because assistant prefilling is removed on the 4.6+ family (it returns HTTP 400) and prefill does not shrink input tokens anyway.

scenario: You're building an invoice-extraction service on claude-sonnet-4-6 that must return a strict JSON object (vendor, total, line_items) with guaranteed schema-valid output for downstream database insertion.
stem: Which approach is the current, documented way to enforce schema-conformant JSON via constrained decoding?

options.text: Set the deprecated output_format parameter to "json" so the API forces valid JSON
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening '{' so the model is forced to continue the JSON object
Set output_config:{format:{type:"json_schema", ...}} with your invoice schema to constrain decoding to that structure
Add "Return only valid JSON, no prose" to the system prompt and text-parse the response for a closing brace to confirm completion

explanation: C is correct: output_config.format with type "json_schema" is the current constrained-decoding mechanism that guarantees output conforms to your schema. A names the deprecated output_format parameter, which is no longer the supported mechanism. B fails because assistant prefilling is removed on the 4.6+ family and returns HTTP 400. D relies on best-effort prompting plus text-parsing to detect completion, which is unreliable—completion should be read from stop_reason, not by scanning content for braces.

scenario: A medical-claims pipeline uses claude-sonnet-4-6 with output_config:{format:{type:"json_schema",...}} to extract patient billing fields into a strict schema. The team assumes constrained decoding alone makes the integration bulletproof and parses every response with JSON.parse without inspecting stop_reason.
stem: Which statement most accurately describes what constrained decoding guarantees and where this pipeline can still break?

options.text: Constrained decoding guarantees both schema-valid JSON and that the model never refuses, so checking stop_reason is unnecessary overhead.
Constrained decoding does not actually enforce the schema; only strict:true tool use does, so the team must switch to tool_use-for-JSON to get any guarantee.
Because output_config enforces the schema, a max_tokens cutoff is impossible during a constrained-decoding response, so truncation cannot occur.

Constrained decoding guarantees emitted tokens conform to the schema, but the response can still be cut off by stop_reason "max_tokens" (yielding incomplete JSON) or returned as stop_reason "refusal" with empty/partial content, so the team must inspect stop_reason before parsing.

explanation: D is correct: constrained decoding constrains the token grammar to the schema, but it cannot prevent a max_tokens truncation (producing incomplete, unparseable JSON) or a "refusal" stop_reason (HTTP 200 with empty/partial content), so stop_reason must be checked before JSON.parse. A is wrong because constrained decoding does not suppress refusals and stop_reason inspection is required, not optional. B is wrong because output_config json_schema is genuine constrained decoding that does enforce the schema; tool use is just an alternative/older pattern, not the only enforcement. C is wrong because max_tokens truncation can absolutely occur mid-output and is a documented stop_reason; schema enforcement does not extend the token budget.

scenario: A team on claude-sonnet-4-6 extracts invoice fields (vendor, total, line_items) from PDFs into a fixed schema. They have no need for any external actions or computation — they only want a guaranteed, typed JSON payload back from the model.
stem: Which approach best fits this extraction goal?

options.text: Use output_config.format with type:"json_schema" so constrained decoding returns the typed payload directly
Define a record_invoice tool with the schema and set tool_choice:"tool" to force a tool_use block containing the JSON
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening '{' to force the model to emit raw JSON
Add the deprecated output_format parameter set to the JSON schema on the request

explanation: A is correct: when the only goal is a typed response payload, output_config.format with json_schema uses constrained decoding to return the structured result directly, avoiding the tool round-trip ceremony. B works but is the older tool_use-for-JSON pattern — forcing a tool just to retrieve data adds a tool_use/tool_result loop you don't need. C is invalid on the 4.6+ family: assistant prefilling is removed and returns HTTP 400. D references the deprecated output_format parameter, which is no longer the supported mechanism.

scenario: Your Customer Support Resolution Agent runs on claude-sonnet-4-6 with output_config.format set to a json_schema (constrained decoding) so each reply emits a structured ticket-resolution object. To keep latency low you set a modest max_tokens, but occasionally the agent emits long resolution summaries and the response comes back with stop_reason "max_tokens".
stem: How should the integration handle these responses so downstream systems never ingest invalid ticket objects?

options.text: Trust that constrained decoding guarantees valid JSON, parse the content directly, and treat any parse exception as a transient network error to retry.

Inspect stop_reason; when it is "max_tokens", treat the output as potentially truncated/invalid JSON—do not parse it as complete—and retry with a higher max_tokens (or otherwise recover) before validating the parsed object against the schema.
Switch back to assistant prefilling by seeding the response with an opening brace to force valid JSON, eliminating the need to check stop_reason.
Scan the raw text for a closing brace; if the final '}' is present, accept the JSON, otherwise append one yourself and parse.

explanation: B is correct: constrained decoding shapes tokens toward the schema, but a max_tokens cutoff can stop generation mid-structure, so the only safe signal is stop_reason—on "max_tokens" you must treat the JSON as possibly truncated, recover (e.g., raise max_tokens), and still validate the parsed object. A is wrong because constrained decoding does not guarantee completeness under truncation, and a JSON parse failure is a content problem, not a network error to blindly retry. C is wrong because assistant prefilling is removed on the 4.6+ family and returns HTTP 400; output_config.format is the supported mechanism. D is wrong because text-parsing for a brace is fragile and you must never detect completion by scanning content—synthetically appending '}' can silently produce structurally-balanced but semantically corrupt data.

scenario: You run a claude-sonnet-4-6 pipeline that extracts invoice line items into a tool called record_invoice, whose input_schema requires fields like total_cents (integer), currency (enum), and a non-empty items array. Downstream services reject malformed payloads, and you currently see occasional runs where Claude emits extra fields, omits required ones, or returns a near-JSON string that fails to parse.
stem: Which approach best guarantees that the tool_use arguments Claude produces always conform to the record_invoice input_schema?

options.text: Keep using the tool but add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to 'only output valid JSON matching the schema and never add extra keys,' then JSON.parse the resulting text block.
Drop the tool entirely and use assistant prefilling with an opening '{' so the model is forced to continue a JSON object matching the schema.
Define the tool with strict:true so the input arguments are constrained-decoded against the input_schema, and read the validated structure from the tool_use block's input.
Set the deprecated output_format parameter to 'json' and parse the assistant's content text, relying on it to align with the tool's schema.

explanation: C is correct: strict:true applies constrained decoding so the tool_use.input is guaranteed to satisfy the declared input_schema (required fields, types, enums), eliminating parse/validation failures. A relies on prompt-only steering, which is best-effort and does not guarantee schema conformance. B is invalid on the 4.6+ family because assistant prefilling is removed and returns HTTP 400. D references the deprecated output_format parameter and, even if it produced JSON, that text is not bound to the tool's schema and must be hand-parsed.

scenario: A team extracts structured invoice records (vendor, line items, totals) from PDFs using claude-sonnet-4-6. Their legacy code prefilled the assistant turn with '{', then text-parsed the response, hand-validated the JSON against a Pydantic model, and re-prompted on validation failures — a brittle manual parse/retry loop that now returns HTTP 400.
stem: Which approach removes the manual parse/retry loop while remaining valid on the current 4.6+ family?

options.text: Drop the prefill and define a strict tool whose input_schema is the invoice model with tool_choice set to tool, then use the SDK's parse helper (Pydantic/Zod) to deserialize the tool_use input directly into a validated object.
Keep prefilling the assistant turn with '{' to force JSON, then pass the text block to model_validate_json() in a try/except retry loop.
Set the deprecated output_format parameter to 'json' and detect completion by checking whether the final content text ends with a closing brace before parsing.
Use a non-strict tool with tool_choice auto and re-prompt whenever the SDK parse helper raises, relying on the model to self-correct malformed fields across turns.

explanation: A is correct: a strict tool (strict:true) with the model as input_schema constrains decoding to valid structure, tool_choice 'tool' forces emission, and SDK parse helpers deserialize the tool_use input straight into a validated object — no manual parse or retry. B fails because assistant prefilling is removed on 4.6+ and returns HTTP 400, and it preserves the very retry loop being eliminated. C is wrong on two counts: output_format is deprecated, and completion must be detected via stop_reason, never by text-inspecting content. D reintroduces a retry loop and, by using a non-strict tool with tool_choice auto, allows unconstrained/malformed output instead of preventing it at decode time.

scenario: Your developer-productivity team is building a Claude-powered code-review assistant on claude-sonnet-4-6. The lead keeps rewriting the system prompt every time a reviewer complains about a false positive, but there is no way to tell whether each edit actually improves quality across the codebase.
stem: What should the team do FIRST to put this on an empirical, eval-first footing?

options.text: Immediately upgrade to claude-opus-4-8 and add high effort thinking, since a stronger model and more reasoning will resolve the false positives without needing measurement.

Assemble a labeled dataset of representative review cases with explicit success criteria, build an automated eval that scores each prompt variant against it, and only then iterate on prompt wording—escalating to a different model or architecture if eval scores plateau.
Add an assistant prefill that forces Claude to begin every review with 'No issues found unless severe:' so it suppresses minor false positives by default.
Ship each prompt edit to production and judge success by manually reading a handful of the next day's reviews to see if they feel better.

explanation: B is correct: an eval-first workflow defines measurable success criteria and an automated scored dataset BEFORE tweaking wording, which makes prompt changes comparable and tells you when the prompt is no longer the lever (plateau) so you escalate model/architecture. A is wrong because it changes the model and effort with no measurement—you can't know if it helped, and it assumes the lever is the model before establishing any baseline. C is wrong because assistant prefilling is removed on Sonnet 4.6 (returns HTTP 400) and steering format/behavior should use system instructions or output_config, not prefill. D is wrong because eyeballing a handful of cases is anecdotal, unrepeatable, and gives no statistical signal across the codebase.

scenario: A multi-agent research system uses a single large prompt that asks claude-sonnet-4-6 to (1) extract claims from 30 source documents, (2) cross-check each claim against the others, and (3) emit a final synthesized report — all in one call. The team finds that when extraction is incomplete, the synthesis silently fabricates coverage, and failures are hard to localize.
stem: Which redesign best improves reliability by introducing verification checkpoints between stages?

options.text: Keep the single prompt but add a final instruction telling Claude to double-check its own work, and parse the response text for the phrase 'verification complete' before accepting the report.
Keep the single prompt and use assistant prefilling to force the model to begin its response with the extraction section, ensuring that stage always runs first.
